title: Determine whether FLOAT(p) precision counts bits or decimal digits
description:
Found 2026-07-26 by team-lead while reviewing the uncommitted gqlc-h9n.16 diff,
before it reached adversarial review. The implementer had extended the bit-width
fold from `binaryExactNumericType` to `approximateNumericType`, folding
`FLOAT(16)` -> `TypeFloat16`. That half was rejected; this bead records the
question it exposed.

## The question

Does the `precision` in `FLOAT(p)` count **bits of mantissa** or **decimal
digits**?

The grammar does not say, and its structure points the wrong way for a
bit-width reading:

```
GQL.g4:1801   INT              (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)?               precision only
GQL.g4:1814   UINT             (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)?               precision only
GQL.g4:1827   INTEGER          (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)?               precision only
GQL.g4:1832   DECIMAL | DEC    (LEFT_PAREN precision (COMMA scale)? RIGHT_PAREN notNull?)?
GQL.g4:1849   FLOAT            (LEFT_PAREN precision (COMMA scale)? RIGHT_PAREN)?
```

`FLOAT`'s parenthetical is identical in shape to `DECIMAL`'s — it carries the
optional `scale`. The criterion that justifies the INT fold (a binary type takes
precision alone; a decimal type pairs precision with scale, which is what
separates `binaryExactNumericType` from `decimalExactNumericType`) therefore
sorts `FLOAT(p)` with the decimal types, not the binary ones.

Against that: `FLOAT16|FLOAT32|FLOAT64|FLOAT128|FLOAT256` are siblings of
`FLOAT (...)` under `approximateNumericType` (GQL.g4:1844-1849), the same
sibling relationship that makes the INT reading work. So the grammar supplies
one argument each way and adjudicates neither.

## Why it matters more than INT(7)

`gqlc-h9n.25` asks what to do about widths with no exact model counterpart.
This is worse, because the plausible-looking fix is **strictly narrowing**:

- Today `FLOAT(16)` -> `TypeFloat` (64-bit). Whatever the author meant, the
  resolved type is a safe superset.
- Folded, `FLOAT(16)` -> `TypeFloat16`. Half precision holds ~3.3 decimal
  digits. If `p` is digits, a schema asking for 16 digits silently resolves to a
  type that holds three.

Strictly-widening is the property demanded of any resolution-rule change on this
epic. A digits reading makes the fold violate it, and the failure is silent —
accepted input, nil error, wrong model, which is this epic's signature defect.
We would be introducing one while fixing another.

## What this bead must produce

An **ISO/IEC 39075 citation**, not an inference. `gqlc-cfj` is open precisely
because this repo has a habit of asserting what the standard says without
sourcing it, and SQL tradition (where `FLOAT(p)` is binary mantissa precision
and has no scale) is not evidence about GQL — note that this grammar gives FLOAT
a scale slot, which SQL's does not, so GQL's FLOAT is demonstrably not SQL's.

Deliverable is one of:

1. Citation says bits -> fold `FLOAT(16..256)` the way INT is folded, in a
   follow-up PR, with the same equivalence test shape.
2. Citation says digits -> record in the `gqlc-0ri` deviation register that
   `FLOAT(p)` is lossy-but-safe, and comment the fallback in
   `internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go` naming it.
3. Standard does not specify -> same as (2), plus say so out loud, because
   silence is itself the finding.

Until then the status quo stands and is pinned: `FLOAT(16)` is a row in
`TestPropertyBinaryWidthNonFolds`, so the decision is asserted by a test rather
than implied by absence.

Scope note: `DECIMAL(p,s)` is not in scope (gqlc-5md owns the length/digit
qualifier question). `INT(7)` and friends are gqlc-h9n.25. This bead is only
about what `FLOAT(p)`'s precision denotes.

title: just: check-hooks warns and exits 0, so dead git hooks read as a green doctor
description:
Found 2026-07-26. Two agents independently hit this within an hour; the second
report is what made the scope clear.

## What was wrong

`core.hooksPath` was set in `.git/config` to the absolute path
`/home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc/.git/hooks`. That directory contains **only
`.sample` files**, which git ignores. So `commit-msg`, `pre-commit`, `pre-push`
and `post-merge` were all inactive — repo-wide, in every worktree, since
`.git/config` is shared by all of them.

Among the casualties: `.githooks/commit-msg`, which CLAUDE.md names as the
enforcement mechanism for the no-AI-attribution rule. CLAUDE.md's claim that the
rule is "enforced at commit time" was simply false for the duration.

Repaired by running `just init` (the project's own recipe:
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks`). Audited the last 40 commits for
`Co-Authored-By:` naming claude/anthropic and for the "Generated with Claude
Code" footer: **zero violations**. Discipline held where the gate did not, but
that is luck, not a control.

## The actual defect — the gate does not gate

`justfile:19` `check-hooks` detects the drift correctly and then does this:

```
echo "warning: core.hooksPath is '${got:-<unset>}', expected '.githooks' — local hooks are inactive. Run 'just init' to fix." >&2
```

It warns and exits 0. Consequences:

- `just doctor` runs `check-hooks` and then prints `ok`. It printed `ok` the
  entire time hooks were dead.
- `check-hooks` is wired into `just test`, where a single stderr line is buried
  in test output nobody reads line-by-line, and the recipe stays green.

So the detector is present, correct, and inert. This is the same shape as
`gqlc-h9n.15` (inert measurement guards) and the CI bead about a workflow that
runs but is not in `required_status_checks` — the mechanism executes and
influences nothing.

The comment above the recipe (justfile:15-17) makes it sharper: it says drift is
"the only way local pre-commit/pre-push gates can silently die (CI cannot see
local git config)". The author identified the exact silent-death mode and then
made the only detector for it non-fatal.

## Fix

Make `check-hooks` exit non-zero on drift. It is already wired into `just test`,
so this converts a buried warning into a hard stop with an actionable message
that already names the remedy (`just init`).

Points to weigh while doing it:

- **`just test` must still be runnable in a fresh clone.** A new contributor who
  has not run `just init` will now hit a hard failure. That is the intent, but
  the message must be unmissable and must lead with the fix. Confirm the failure
  text renders well when `just test` fails on it.
- **Does anything in CI run `check-hooks`?** CI has no local hooks and does not
  need them. If `just test` is invoked in CI, a hard failure there would be a
  self-inflicted outage. Check `ci.yml` before changing the exit status, and if
  CI does call it, make the check conditional on not-CI rather than weakening it.
  This is the load-bearing question — get it wrong and the fix breaks the build.
- **Mutation-test the fix**: unset `core.hooksPath`, set it to a wrong path, and
  set it to a path of `.sample`-only files. The third is the case that actually
  occurred and the one a naive "is it set?" check would miss. The current
  string-equality check against `.githooks` happens to catch it; do not
  regress that into an existence test.

## Follow-up worth considering, not required here

`check-hooks` compares the config value to the literal string `.githooks`. That
is right, but it does not verify the hooks are executable or that the directory
is non-empty. A `core.hooksPath = .githooks` pointing at a directory whose files
lost their executable bit would pass. Cheap to add while in there; do not let it
expand the change.
close_reason: Landed in PR #417. check-hooks now exits 1 on core.hooksPath drift, skipped under CI (ci.yml:51 runs 'just test' in a fresh clone where the value is unset, so a naive fatal check would have broken every CI run). Kept the value comparison rather than a directory-existence test — .git/hooks exists and holds only .sample files, so an existence test cannot see this failure; a justfile comment records that. Mutation-verified across four states: correct value, CI=true, drift to the absolute .git/hooks path that actually occurred, and unset. 'just doctor' now exits 1 on drift instead of printing ok. Audited the 40 commits made while hooks were dead for AI-attribution trailers and footers: zero violations.

title: schema/gql: EnterNodeTypePattern has no nesting-depth guard
description:
`closedGraphReferenceValueType` (`internal/grammar/gql/GQL.g4:1926`) is
`PROPERTY? GRAPH nestedGraphTypeSpecification notNull?` — a whole graph type body
can appear as a **property value type**. `EnterNodeTypePattern`
(`internal/schema/gql/listener.go:109`) appends to `l.raw.nodes` unconditionally,
with no check on how deeply nested the pattern is. Element types declared inside
a nested specification are therefore collected as element types of the **outer**
graph type.

The test harness already models the correct rule: `coverage.nestingDepth`
(`internal/schema/gql/corpus_coverage_test.go:128`) counts enclosing
`nestedGraphTypeSpecification` contexts precisely so it can tell "an element of
this graph type" from "an element of one nested inside a property". The listener
has no equivalent.

## Status: latent, not live — and the failure shape is worse than a leak

Measured at `7217b18` by walking the listener directly and reading `l.raw`:

```
CREATE GRAPH TYPE Seed {
    (:Outer { g :: PROPERTY GRAPH { (:Inner), (:Inner2) } })
}
```

```
walk err = unsupported property value type
raw.nodes collected = 2
  [0] name="" alias="" labels=[Inner]  props=0
  [1] name="" alias="" labels=[Inner2] props=0
```

Note what that is. It is not "outer plus two extra". `Outer` is **absent** and the
two nested nodes have been **promoted to top level** — the collection is inverted.
`EnterNodeTypePattern` returns early without appending when `nodeContent` fails, so
the one real node is dropped, while the two nodes that should not exist at this
level are appended by their own (successful) `EnterNodeTypePattern` calls.

Nothing of this is observable today: `walk` returns
`ErrUnsupportedPropertyValueType`, so `resolve()` never runs and `Parse` returns a
zero schema with a non-nil error. The behaviour is correct by accident, via a
rejection that has nothing to do with nesting.

## Why this needs fixing before the value type is supported, not after

The masking error is exactly what a later bead will remove. The moment
`closedGraphReferenceValueType` is accepted, this becomes a live silent wrong
answer of the worst shape in this epic — a *partial and wrong* schema with a `nil`
error, where the declared node is missing and two undeclared ones are present.

So: add the depth guard now, while it is cheap and provable in isolation, rather
than discovering it as a regression inside the value-type work.

## Fix

Give the listener the same notion of depth the coverage harness has, and ignore
element types at depth > 0 in `EnterNodeTypePattern` and its edge counterpart.
Whether nested element types should eventually be *modelled* is a separate
question; the immediate requirement is that they must not silently become
elements of the enclosing graph type.

Guard it with a test that walks the listener and asserts on `raw`, not only on
`Parse` — a `Parse`-level test cannot see this while the value type is rejected,
and a test that passes for the wrong reason is how this survived in the first
place.

Discovered while reviewing PR #392.

title: schema/gql: properties on an inline endpoint node reference are parsed and discarded
description:
`sourceNodeTypeReference` and `destinationNodeTypeReference` each have an
alternative 2 of the form `LEFT_PAREN nodeTypeFiller? RIGHT_PAREN`
(`internal/grammar/gql/GQL.g4:1640-1646`). That filler admits a full property
type set. The listener parses it and throws it away.

Measured at `7217b18` with a scratch probe:

```
(:Person) -[:AUTHORED]-> (:Post { extra :: STRING })
```

```
endpoint_props             err=nil nodes=2 edges=1 | Person:props=1 Post:props=1
baseline_plain_endpoints   err=nil nodes=2 edges=1 | Person:props=1 Post:props=1
```

The two spellings resolve **byte-identically**: `extra` is discarded and the error
is `nil`. This is the same silent-wrong-answer shape the corpus work was built to
eliminate, surviving inside a construct the gate reads as covered.

## Why the gate does not catch it

Coverage is measured on the **parse tree**. ANTLR entering the subtree discharges
the obligation whether or not the listener then reads anything from it. So
`sourceNodeTypeReference#2` is green at `alternatives 46/46` while its contents are
dropped. `assertNothingDropped` does not help either: it compares *element* counts —
three declarations, three model entries — and never looks at properties.

This is a live witness that "133/133/46" and "no silent drops" are different
statements. Worth keeping that framing when fixing it.

## Fix

Decide the semantics first. An inline endpoint filler either

- (a) declares properties on the endpoint node type, in which case it must merge
  with, or conflict-check against, the node type declared elsewhere in the same
  graph type; or
- (b) is a constraint the model has no room for, in which case it is a
  `semanticCase` and must be **rejected** with a sentinel rather than accepted and
  dropped.

Either way the current behaviour — accept, discard, return nil — is not one of the
options. Reject-with-sentinel is the cheap correct step if (a) is not wanted yet;
that converts a silent wrong answer into a named gap, which is the sequencing the
epic already uses everywhere else.

Add corpus coverage for the property-bearing endpoint spelling; the corpus today
reaches the alternative only with an empty filler.

Discovered while reviewing PR #392.

title: schema/gql: gate the incidental-carrier class in the corpus coverage test
description:
The corpus-wide coverage gate asks whether *some* corpus file reaches a grammar
name, never *which* file. So a name can read green because a file in an unrelated
clause area reached it in passing. That is the **incidental-carrier** class, and it
is invisible to `TestCorpusGrammarCoverage` by construction.

Two instances were found and fixed by hand on the `gqlc-h9n.2` branch (PR #392):

1. `localdatetimeType#2` (`TIMESTAMP (WITHOUT TIME ZONE)? notNull?`) was reached
   only by five `18.3-edge-type` files that used `TIMESTAMP` as a property type in
   examples that are not about type grammar at all. Fixed by adding
   `18.9-value-type/scalar_timestamp.gql` and
   `scalar_timestamp_without_time_zone.gql` so the value-type area carries its own
   spellings.
2. Every corpus file spelling the `NODE` keyword was an `unsupported` entry — both
   18.2 phrase forms and `constructed_node_open` — so no *resolving* path exercised
   an explicit node synonym in `nodeTypePattern`, even though the `VERTEX` spelling
   of the same production had resolved all along. Fixed by
   `12.6-graph-type-statement/synonyms_node_edge.gql`.

## The actual defect

**Nothing in the tree gates any of this.** Delete either fix, repin
`wantCorpusEntries` / `wantCorpusResolving`, and the suite is green again at
`rules 133/133, tokens 133/133, alternatives 46/46` — carriage silently reverts to
the incidental files. The three `.gql` files that close the two instances are held
in place by a header comment, not by a test.

The measurement itself was also by hand, at one SHA, and is not reproducible from
the tree: the detector lives in `/tmp/lead/orphans.sh` and was never checked in.

## What to build

Move the per-area detector into the package as a test. The method that worked:

- Derive the full obligation set once by running the closure with an empty corpus.
- For each area, keep only that area's files and run the gate; `carried(area)` is
  the obligation set minus the red set.
- A name whose owning area is not among its carriers is an orphan.

Guard rails that mattered while building it out of tree, and that a real test gets
for free: the copy step must not nest (`cp -r src dst` nests when `dst` exists —
this produced two byte-identical runs at two different SHAs and was caught only by
validating against a SHA with a known orphan), and `go test -count=1` is mandatory
because the corpus files are out-of-module inputs the build cache does not see.

Validation requirement: the new test must be shown non-vacuous by pointing it at
the commit before either fix and confirming it independently reproduces that
orphan.

## Scope note

Deciding *which* area owns a name is the hard part and is a judgement call for
cross-cutting productions (`notNull` is reached by every area). The out-of-tree
detector resolved this by directory prefix on the corpus path. That is good enough
and should be kept; where it is wrong, an explicit exemption list with a reason
per entry is preferable to loosening the rule.

Discovered while reviewing PR #392.

title: schema/gql: parenthesised numeric width spellings lose their width — INTEGER(8) resolves to INT, not INT8
description:
RE-SCOPED 2026-07-26 to Problem A only. The length/precision/scale half moved to
gqlc-5md; see "What moved out and why" at the bottom.

## Problem A: the width fold

Measured 2026-07-25 (probe /tmp/h9n2probe/leadstrlen) and re-measured 2026-07-26
(probe /tmp/h9n16-probe, complete files, Parse + model compare).

All six numeric width pairs diverge. The suffix spelling keeps the width; the
parenthesised spelling of the SAME construct loses it:

  INT8    -> INT8     but  INTEGER(8)  -> INT
  INT16   -> INT16    but  INTEGER(16) -> INT
  INT32   -> INT32    but  INTEGER(32) -> INT
  INT64   -> INT64    but  INTEGER(64) -> INT
  FLOAT32 -> FLOAT32  but  FLOAT(32)   -> FLOAT
  FLOAT64 -> FLOAT64  but  FLOAT(64)   -> FLOAT

`INTEGER(8)` emits Go `int` where the schema said 8 bits. ADR 0002's own
rationale condemns exactly this:

  "Losing signedness and width would force codegen to emit int/uint everywhere
   and discard information the schema author explicitly stated."

So Problem A is a defect *against a recorded decision*, not a change *to* one.
That is the whole reason it separates cleanly from gqlc-5md.

## Root cause

`internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go:canonicalSpelling` truncates the spelling at
the first `(` before the `typeSpellings` lookup runs. `INTEGER(8)` is looked up as
`INTEGER`, which is a real row, so the lookup succeeds and returns `TypeInt`. The
parameter is not "dropped for lack of a field" — it is discarded before anything
could read it.

## Measured equivalence classes (2026-07-26)

  TYPE=STRING <- STRING | STRING(10) | STRING(2, 5) | STRING(0xFF) | CHAR |
                 CHAR(4) | CHAR(8) | VARCHAR | VARCHAR(5)
  TYPE=INT    <- INT | INT(8) | INT(10) | INT(16) | INT(32) | INT(64) | INT(7) |
                 INTEGER | INTEGER(8) | INTEGER(10)
  TYPE=INT8   <- INT8 | INTEGER8

Only the width-bearing members of these classes move under Problem A. The
STRING class does not change at all — it is gqlc-5md's problem.

## Mechanism (no new field, no new code path)

- `internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go`: 23 new `typeSpellings` rows; make
  `canonicalSpelling` normalise whitespace *inside* the parenthetical; make
  `normaliseType` try the full canonical spelling first and fall back to today's
  truncated lookup.
- `internal/schema/gql/propertytype_test.go`: a table pinning the 23 folds AND
  the non-folds — INT(7), INT(10), FLOAT(24), FLOAT(10, 2), DEC(8), STRING(5) —
  because the fallback is the half that can silently over-reach.
- `docs/adr/0002-bit-width-preserving-value-type-model.md`: amend the
  normalisation sentence so the width-bearing parenthetical is named as folding,
  distinct from the length/precision qualifier that still drops.
- Re-point the five corpus rows citing `bead: "gqlc-h9n.16"` to `gqlc-5md`.
  Nothing checks that a cited bead is open, so this must land in THIS PR.

## NOT strictly widening — the PR body must say so

- Codegen: 13 emissions change text; 9 spellings go from generating to
  `ErrUnrepresentableWidth`, which aborts the WHOLE schema generation at
  `internal/codegen/prepare.go:489`; 1 no-op. `INT(128)` emits `Amount int`
  today and will abort generation after the fold.
- Resolver: `INT8` vs `INT(8)` unions start passing (widening). `INT(8)` vs
  `INT(16)` unions that pass today start FAILING. That is the one genuine
  regression and it is intended — the two are different widths.

## Do not sub-split

Do not stage this as "fold 8/16/32/64 now, 128/256 later". Leaving 128/256
unfolded preserves `INT(128)` != `INT128`, which is the divergence this bead
exists to close, and buys only a deferral of a regression that has to be taken
eventually.

## Ordering

gqlc-h9n.21 (assert the model collision a semanticCase describes, not just its
spelling) must land before gqlc-5md. It does NOT block Problem A: zero corpus
entries and zero semantic rows change under Problem A.

## What moved out and why

The length/precision/scale field on PropertyType is now gqlc-5md at P3.
ADR 0002 states verbatim that "length and precision qualifiers (VARCHAR(255),
DECIMAL(p,s)) are dropped", and `TestPropertyLengthQualifiersDropped`
(internal/schema/gql/propertytype_test.go:108) pins that with five rows and a
doc comment citing the ADR. Adding the field is therefore a REVERSAL of a
recorded decision, not a bug fix, and it needs a named consumer to justify it.
Problem A needs neither.

## Why this bead matters beyond itself

Structurally the same defect family as gqlc-uhb (phrase forms silently dropped)
-- accepted input, nil error, wrong model -- which is the family the h9n corpus
epic exists to find. The corpus manifest cannot express it: such a file's outcome
is `resolves` and the coverage gate is satisfied, because coverage is measured
from the parse tree and the parse tree is correct. Detecting this class needs a
model assertion, not a coverage one. See gqlc-h9n.13.

title: schema/gql: corpus size pins block every corpus author
description:
TestCorpusManifest ends with two count pins:

    require.Len(t, entries, wantCorpusEntries, "corpus size changed; repin wantCorpusEntries")
    require.Equal(t, wantCorpusResolving, resolving, "resolving count changed; repin wantCorpusResolving")

wantCorpusEntries / wantCorpusResolving are consts in corpus_test.go -- a SHARED file. The
corpus authors own only their own corpus_area_<X>_test.go plus .gql files, and the author
brief tells all five that "TestCorpusManifest and TestCorpusOutcomes must pass outright" as
their done-signal.

Those two facts contradict each other. An author cannot add a single corpus file without
failing TestCorpusManifest, and cannot fix it without editing a file they are forbidden to
touch. VERIFIED, not reasoned: simulated one author adding one .gql plus one area-file entry
and touching no shared file, in a scratch copy of the worktree --

    --- FAIL: TestCorpusManifest (0.00s)
        corpus_test.go:274: corpus: 10 entries, 5 resolving
        Messages: corpus size changed; repin wantCorpusEntries

TestCorpusOutcomes passed, so it is specifically the count pins.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE NOISE. The failure message says "repin wantCorpusEntries",
which instructs the author to do the one forbidden thing. Five authors each bumping 9 to
9+their own count is a five-way conflict on a single line whose correct value none of them
can know, in the one file the area split exists to keep uncontended. The alternative
outcomes are five duplicate messages to team-lead, or an author concluding the harness is
broken and stopping.

FIX, prototyped and verified in /tmp/goldencheck, diff at /tmp/lead/patch/corpus_test.go.diff:
move both pins out of TestCorpusManifest into a new TestCorpusSize. The two tests answer
questions with different lifetimes -- the manifest checks are invariants (every file has an
entry, every unsupported entry names a real sentinel), while the counts are regression pins
that are stale by design the moment anyone adds a file. Verified both directions:

    author adds a file, runs their done-signal:
        go test -run 'TestCorpusManifest|TestCorpusOutcomes'   -> ok
    and the regression pin still fires, carrying the repin to team-lead:
        go test -run TestCorpusSize   -> FAIL  corpus size changed; repin wantCorpusEntries

Do NOT delete the pins instead. wantCorpusResolving is a real guard: an author converting a
resolves entry to unsupported to make their life easier is a regression the ElementsMatch
checks cannot see, and "a drop is a regression" is the note that catches it.

Must land BEFORE the five author worktrees are cut, since they branch from that commit.
close_reason: Landed in PR #392 (squash 6d4ac8f). Corpus size pins no longer block parallel authors.

title: resolver: label expression must resolve by satisfaction and union, not exact label-set lookup
description:
`internal/resolver/resolve.go:184-187` resolves a query's node label to a schema
node type by **exact map lookup** on `LabelSetKey` — the sorted, deduped,
`&`-joined canonicalisation of the type's *complete* label set. So a pattern can
only ever match a node type whose full label set is spelled identically.

That is wrong. A label expression is satisfied by an element whose label set is a
**superset**, and it resolves to the **union** of every node type that satisfies
it.

Verified 2026-07-25:

    CREATE GRAPH TYPE G AS {
      NODE TYPE Person (p :Person&Employee {id STRING, name STRING, joined_date DATE}),
      DIRECTED EDGE TYPE K (p)-[:KNOWS {since INT}]->(p)
    }

    match (p1:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(p2:Person) ... 

    internal/user/db/user.cypher: query T: unknown label: Person

A node of type `Person&Employee` **does** carry the label `Person`, so the
pattern must match it. It does not.

## Why this is the most serious defect in the epic

Subclause 16.8 `<label expression>` carries **no Annex D feature ID**, which per
Neo4j's conformance appendix means it is **mandatory**, not optional. Every other
item in this epic is an optional feature that gqlc may legitimately decline. This
one it may not.

CITED: *Graph Pattern Matching in GQL and SQL/PGQ*, SIGMOD 2022 (arXiv
2112.06217), authored by the GQL editors — "`MATCH (x:Account)` … only nodes with
the label Account will now be bound to x"; `&`, `|`, `!`, `%` supported. The
expression is evaluated over an element's **data** label set, never against
declared type identities.

It is also wrong under plain openCypher semantics, where `(p:Person)` likewise
means "has label Person", so this is not a GQL-vs-Cypher nuance. The bug is
language-agnostic.

## Two things are conflated

Per the key-label-set research (see the `gqlc-iso-node-type-identity` bd
memory), ISO GQL separates the **key label set** (identity, the part before `=>`)
from the **complete label set** (what conforming data must carry). `LabelSet.Key`
is a fine canonicalisation of the latter and an illegitimate stand-in for the
former. Fixing satisfaction and fixing identity are related but separable: this
bead is satisfaction only, and is deliberately scoped to leave identity keyed as
it is today so it can land on its own.

## Resolution must be a union, and a union can be empty or plural

- zero satisfying node types -> the existing unknown-label error, but phrased as
  "no node type satisfies" rather than "unknown label"
- exactly one -> today's behaviour
- more than one -> a new decision. The properties available on the binding are
  those common to all members, and a property present in only some members must
  not type-check. This is the part that needs design, not just a lookup change.

The plural case is reachable today without any `=>` support: two node types that
merely share a label (`(:Person&Employee)` and `(:Person&Contractor)`) are enough.
design:
# gqlc-h9n.7 — label satisfaction and the plural case

Design note. Read-only research at `origin/master` `7518581`. Probes:
`/tmp/h9n7/scratch/probe{,2,3,4,6}/main.go`. Full output:
`/tmp/h9n7/probe-output.txt` (every claim below is a line in it).

---

## 0. Three corrections to the brief

**(a) The bug is broader than the bead says.** It is not "`:Person` misses
`(:Person&Employee)`" — *no* proper subset of a declared label set resolves.
`match (p:Employee) return p.salary` also fails with `unknown label: Employee`.
So writing any `NODE TYPE X (:A&B)` makes **both** `A` and `B` unusable as
query labels.

**(b) The query spelling is `:A:B`; `&` does not parse.** `match
(p:Person&Employee)` is a *parse* error (`token recognition error at: '&'`), as
is `|`. Only openCypher conjunction `:A:B` works. So the query parser has no
label-expression surface at all — just a label *set* — and satisfaction reduces
to `declared ⊇ queried`, a subset test, not an expression evaluator. The bead
cites SIGMOD 2022 for `&`/`|`/`!`/`%`; those are Cypher-grammar work, not
resolver work. **The bead should say so** — "implement §16.8" and "make subset
matching work" are very different sizes, and only the latter is in its
acceptance criteria.

**(c) The plural design already exists in the tree, on the edge side.** R3
shipped `edgeCands` / `ResolvedEdgeUnion` / `unionProperty`, and
`unionProperty` (`resolve.go:731`) implements *exactly* the rule the bead
proposes as new. Verified: `r.w` (on both, same type) resolves; `r.only` (on
one) → `unknown property: ... missing on union member A-[S]->B`; `r.skew`
(`INT` vs `STRING`) → `unknown property: ... type differs across union
members`. The owner's position is therefore not a new commitment; it is the
already-shipped edge semantics, and the node side should match it.

---

## 1. What intersection means for generated code (Q1)

Schema: `Employee (e :Person&Employee {id, name, salary INT})` and
`Contractor (c :Person&Contractor {id, name, agency STRING})`.

**1a. `RETURN p.name` — free.** Intersection collapses to one
`ResolvedProperty{STRING}` before codegen sees anything. `phaseAAdmit`
(`prepare.go:571`) and `phaseBDerive` (`:690`) map it to a `*string` row field.
**Zero codegen change.** The whole implementation is `unionProperty` with
`[]schema.NodeType` in place of `[]schema.EdgeKey`.

**1b. Same name, different type → error.** Precedent, not preference: the edge
lane already errors (`resolve.go:744`, `r.skew` above). Narrowing is
unavailable — `graph.PropertyType` is a bit-width-preserving enum (ADR 0002)
with no join. Note the existing check compares `Type` **and** `Nullable`, so
`STRING` vs `STRING NOT NULL` also errors. Copy it verbatim; do not invent a
nullability lattice.

**1c. `RETURN p` — the real problem.** `ResolvedNode` carries exactly one
`LabelSetKey` (`validated.go:89`), and codegen resolves it via
`entityIndex[{entityNode, t.Labels}]` (`prepare.go:576, :698`) into one struct
per declared node type. A plural binding has no single key.

The edge side solves this with a synthesised sealed interface — verified
emission for `RETURN r` on `[r:R|S]` is `type TR interface{ isTR() }`, marker
methods `func (R) isTR() {}`, and a `switch rel.Type` in the query method.
**Copying that for nodes does not work, and this is the finding I most want
you to see.** The edge dispatch is total because `dbtype.Relationship.Type` is
a `string` and a relationship has exactly one type. The node discriminator is
`dbtype.Node.Labels []string` — a **set** — and under the very
superset-satisfaction rule this bead introduces, one runtime node can satisfy
two declared types at once: a node labelled `{Person, Employee, Contractor}`
conforms to both `Person&Employee` and `Person&Contractor`. No principled
`switch` arm exists; "first match wins" makes the emitted struct depend on
slice order.

That rules out one design, not the plural case. Three options remain:

| | emits | works? | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(a) sealed interface** | interface + label dispatch | **no** — ambiguous discriminator | — |
| **(b) intersection struct** | per-query struct with only common properties | yes, and total — no dispatch needed | a **new codegen entity kind**: naming rule, decode fn, collision check vs schema entity names |
| **(c) refuse** | a resolver diagnostic | yes | one sentinel + one fixture |

To be accurate: (b) is the literal reading of your stated rule and it is *not*
blocked, only expensive. It also silently drops `salary`/`agency` from the row
— defensible for a property projection, surprising for a whole-entity one.

---

## 2. Intersection or error? (Q2) — recommendation

**Neither as posed. Split on projection shape, not on plurality:** plural +
property → **intersection**; plural + whole-entity → **refuse** (option c),
leaving (b) as a wideable follow-up.

1. **The brief's "reject anything plural" alternative fails its own goal.**
   `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name` is the most ordinary query in the language.
   Under blanket rejection it compiles or not depending on whether some *other*
   type the query never mentions shares a label — a colleague adding `NODE TYPE
   Contractor` breaks your build. The property path must work.
2. **The property path costs zero downstream** (§1a).
3. **Refusing is wideable; shipping (b) is not.** A rejected query later being
   accepted breaks nobody. Emitting an intersection struct and later preferring
   a discriminated shape *is* breaking — user code has named the type.
4. **Shape-specific refusal inside `refProjectionType` is an existing
   pattern.** `scope.go:698` already refuses *property* projection on a
   var-length edge while permitting the whole-entity one, with a message naming
   the alternative route. Same function, same posture, opposite axis.
5. The bead's acceptance criteria only bind the property case; (c) satisfies
   the bead as written, (b) exceeds it.

---

## 3. Edges (Q3) — your suspicion is right, for a sharper reason

**3a. The `Label` component: same shape, currently worse than nodes.**
`EdgeKey.Label` is a full `LabelSetKey` and edge types really can be
multi-label (`schema/gql/resolve.go:65`). But **no query spelling reaches
one**: `:KNOWS` misses `FOLLOWS&KNOWS`; `:KNOWS:FOLLOWS` does not parse (Cypher
edges take `|`, not `:`); `:KNOWS|FOLLOWS` is alternation of two singletons,
both missing. `edgeCandidates` (`resolve.go:471`) hardcodes the singleton by
building `graph.LabelSet{L}.Key()` per label. A multi-label edge type is
**dead** — a stricter statement than the bead makes, and worth its own bead.
The fix itself is the same subset compare as nodes.

**3b. The endpoints: harder, and *forced* by the node fix.** This is worse than
"materially harder" — **you cannot fix nodes and defer edges.**
`endpointLabels` (`resolve.go:503`) returns exactly one `LabelSetKey` from
`resolved[v].Labels`. The moment a node binding is plural it has no single key
to return, and `closeEdge` / `edgeCandidates` / `candidateTypes` /
`describeTriedEdges` all consume that single-key output. So `scope.nodeTypes`
must become a candidate lane mirroring `edgeCands` in the same change.

Counted ripple: 20 `nodeTypes[...]` sites in non-test code. 13 are
presence-only (`_, ok :=`) and survive untouched. **7 read the value and must
each decide what plural means**: `scope.go:144` (BindNode's identity compare),
`:654` (`refProjectionType`), `:807` (`Export`), `:918`
(`PropertyUseWitness`), `resolve.go:972`/`:1057`/`:1130` (SET/REMOVE/DELETE
validators) — plus `endpointLabels:503`.

Conceptually it composes cleanly once nodes expose a set ("is `Person&Employee`
in the satisfying set of `{Person}`?" is the same predicate reused); the cost
is a cross-product in `edgeCandidates`, which is fine — schemas are small and
the code is already naive-iteration by choice (`resolve.go:1166`).

---

## 4. Blast radius (Q4)

**Small, and nothing pins the bug.**

- **No resolver fixture schema uses a multi-label node type** — `grep -l "&"
  test/data/resolver/*/schemas/*.gql` is empty across all 8 schemas. No valid
  golden changes; no invalid fixture flips.
- **All six `ErrUnknownLabel` fixtures stay red for the right reason** —
  `unknown_label`, `create_unknown_label`, `merge_endpoint_unknown_label`,
  `union_unknown_label_branch`, `set_labels_undeclared`,
  `remove_labels_undeclared` all name a label declared nowhere, which satisfies
  nothing under the new rule too. **None pins the bug.** Only their *messages*
  move, and the string-level assertions are
  `internal/cli/pipeline/pipeline_test.go:308,442,444,445,478` and
  `internal/cli/generate_test.go:321` (`"unknown label: Ghost"`).
- **`TestSentinelReachability`** (`resolver_test.go:285`) plus `TestInvalid`'s
  two totality assertions (`:262-263`) mean a new sentinel needs a fixture *and*
  entries in `invalidFixtures` and `schema.mapping.json`. That is the gate.
- **Codegen already refuses part of the space:** `ErrUnnamedMultiLabelType`
  (`prepare.go:408`) rejects *unnamed* multi-label node types, so every plural
  member is guaranteed an explicit name — which is what makes (b) namable.
- **A ready-made plural fixture already exists**:
  `test/data/schema/gql/valid/node_types_only.gql` declares both `(:Person …)`
  and `(:Person&Employee …)`. Schema-parse-only today; the obvious donor.

**Anything asserting the wrong thing?** No test pins the bug. The closest wrong
assertion is documentation: `errors.go:12-15` describes `ErrUnknownLabel` as
firing when a label set "does not resolve to a declared node type" — exact
lookup written up as if intended. That comment must change with the behaviour.

---

## 5. One error or two? (Q5)

**One sentinel for the two label diagnostics; a new one for the plural
refusal.**

- `ErrUnknownLabel` is *already* overloaded across five fail-sites (its own
  docstring enumerates them). The house discipline is clearly not one sentinel
  per message.
- The in-file precedent is `ErrUnknownProperty`, which distinguishes `"missing
  on union member"` from `"type differs across union members"`
  (`resolve.go:737, :745`) — two faults, one sentinel, message carries it.
- `TestSentinelReachability` prices each new sentinel at a fixture plus two map
  entries. Worth it when a caller branches; none does here — the CLI formats
  the message (`pipeline_test.go` asserts strings, not `errors.Is`).
- The branch predicate **already exists**: `labelDeclared` (`resolve.go:1168`),
  R6's per-label-component check. Note the latent inconsistency it exposes —
  R6's SET/REMOVE label validation is already satisfaction-shaped while Phase
  A1's is exact-key-shaped. They should agree after this bead.

```
some label undeclared → "unknown label: %s is not declared on any node type"
all declared, none satisfies → "no node type satisfies %s; declared types carrying these labels: <list>"
```

The plural refusal is a different fault with a different fix, needs a fixture
anyway, and overloading it onto `ErrUnknownLabel` would make that sentinel mean
both "too few" and "too many". `ErrAmbiguousBinding` is tempting but its
documented meaning is *inference* failure at Phase B; this is a
*representation* failure at the projection walk. New sentinel.

---

## 6. Does this need an ADR? (Q6)

**Yes — for the plural decision, not the lookup fix.** The lookup fix is a bug
fix; bead plus spec note suffices. The plural decision picks a permanent shape
for the type model that, per ADR 0010, leaks into generated code users name.
ADR 0006's core argument — "the conservative default is safe because relaxing
later is non-breaking and the reverse is not" — decides this one too, which is
a good sign it belongs in the same series. 0006 is 64 lines; this needn't be
long.

> A query label expression resolves to the **set** of declared node types whose
> label set is a superset of it. Where that set is plural, a **property**
> reference resolves to the intersection — identical name, type and nullability
> across every member, else `ErrUnknownProperty` — reusing the rule R3 already
> applies to multi-candidate edges; a **whole-entity** reference is
> **rejected**, because the generated decode would have to discriminate on
> `dbtype.Node.Labels`, a set, and one node can conform to two declared types at
> once, so no total dispatch exists.
>
> Rejection is chosen over synthesising a per-query intersection struct because
> widening a rejected query to an accepted one is non-breaking, while replacing
> an emitted struct later is not.

---

## 7. What I would do next

1. **Bead 1 (small, lands now).** Subset matching, singular results only: 1 →
   today's behaviour; 0 → reworded diagnostic; ≥2 → new sentinel, refuse.
   **Fixes the bead's verbatim repro.** Touches `resolve.go:184-188`, errors,
   fixtures. No representation change, no edge change, no codegen change.
2. **Bead 2.** Plural property intersection. Pluralises `scope.nodeTypes`,
   drags `endpointLabels` and the 7 value-reading sites. The ADR lands here.
3. **Bead 3 (new, found here).** Multi-label edge types are unreachable from
   any query spelling (§3a). Not covered by gqlc-h9n.7 as written.
acceptance_criteria:
A query label matches every node type whose label set contains it, so MATCH (p:Person) resolves against a node type declared (:Person&Employee).
Zero satisfying node types produces an error phrased as 'no node type satisfies', naming the expression and the declared types.
Exactly one satisfying node type behaves as today.
More than one satisfying node type has a designed, documented and tested outcome; a property present on only some members does not type-check.
Edge label resolution gets the same treatment as node label resolution.
The plural case is covered by a fixture using two node types that share a label, with no => support required.
notes:
## Design landed; scope narrowed to step 1 (team-lead decision, 2026-07-26)

Full design note attached as the issue's design field. Read it before starting;
it is dense and every claim in it was probed, not reasoned. Headlines:

- **The bug is broader than this bead said.** It is not "`:Person` cannot match
  `(:Person&Employee)`". *No proper subset of any declared label set resolves.*
  Writing `NODE TYPE X (:A&B)` makes both `A` and `B` unusable as query labels.
- **Scope correction: `|`, `!`, `%` are NOT in scope.** The query parser accepts
  conjunction only, spelled openCypher-style `:A:B` — `:A&B` is a lexer error.
  So satisfaction reduces to a subset test, `declared ⊇ queried`, not a label
  *expression* evaluator. "Implement §16.8 label expressions" and "make subset
  matching work" are very different sizes and only the latter is wanted here.
- **Intersection semantics are already shipped, on the edge side.**
  `unionProperty` (`resolve.go:731`) implements the exact rule this bead
  proposes as new. Reuse it verbatim; "common" means same name **and** type
  **and** nullability (`resolve.go:744`), which is already enforced there. Do
  not invent a nullability lattice.
- **You cannot fix nodes and defer edges.** `endpointLabels` (`resolve.go:503`)
  returns exactly one `LabelSetKey`; the moment a node binding can be plural it
  has no single key to return, and `closeEdge` / `edgeCandidates` /
  `candidateTypes` / `describeTriedEdges` all consume that. 20 `nodeTypes[...]`
  sites, 13 presence-only and survive, **7 must decide what plural means**.
  That ripple is why this bead splits.

### This bead is now step 1 only

Subset matching that **stays singular**. Compute the satisfying set at
`resolve.go:184-188`; 1 → today's behaviour; 0 → reworded diagnostic; >=2 →
refuse with a new sentinel. No representation change, no edge change, no
codegen change, no ADR. It fixes this bead's verbatim repro.

### One correction to the design, and it is load-bearing

The design's step 1 as written **ships a regression**, and the fixture that
proves it is already in the tree. `test/data/schema/gql/valid/node_types_only.gql`
declares *both* `(:Person {...})` and `(:Person&Employee {...})`. So for the
query `MATCH (p:Person)` the satisfying set is **{Person, Person&Employee} —
size 2** — and "≥2 → refuse" would fail a query that resolves fine today via
the exact-key lookup at `s.Nodes[key]`.

**Decision: an exact label-set match wins outright.** Resolution order is
(1) exact match on the declared key → done, plural test never runs;
(2) otherwise the proper-superset satisfying set, with the 1/0/>=2 rule above.
That is the ordinary most-specific-declaration-wins rule and it makes step 1
strictly widening — no query that compiles today stops compiling.

A regression test built on exactly this shape (a bare `(:Person)` alongside a
`(:Person&Employee)`, querying `:Person`) is **required**, not optional. It is
the one case where the naive reading of "satisfaction" breaks a working query.

Noted for step 2, not step 1: a runtime node labelled `{Person, Employee}` does
match the pattern `(:Person)` and will be decoded as the `Person` struct,
dropping `employeeId`/`title`. That unsoundness exists today and step 1 neither
adds nor removes it. It belongs in the step-2 ADR.

## Correction to my own note above (team-lead, 2026-07-26)

My "Decision: an exact label-set match wins outright" stands, and the
implementation follows it. But **my stated justification was partly wrong** and
should not be carried forward.

I wrote that ">=2 -> refuse would fail a query that resolves fine today" and
that "the fixture proving it is already in the tree". The behavioural claim is
right; the *fixture* claim is not. `test/data/schema/gql/valid/node_types_only.gql`
is **schema-parse-only** — no resolver query runs against it — and no schema
under `test/data/resolver/{valid,invalid}/schemas/` declares `&` at all. So no
existing test would have gone red. The naive rule would have shipped a silent
behavioural regression with a green suite, which is worse than what I described,
not better.

The correct and stronger justification: exact precedence **preserves observable
behaviour exactly**, making step 1 strictly widening. Verified by probe against
that schema (declared keys `[Company Employee&Person Person Tag]`):

    match (p:Person) return p.email          -> OK, STRING nullable
    match (p:Person:Employee) return p.title -> OK
    match (p:Employee) return p.title        -> unknown label: Employee   <- the bug

So precedence is the status quo, not a new invention.

Recorded because a tracker entry with a false reason is the same defect this
epic exists to remove, and because the difference matters for step 2: see
gqlc-h9n.22, where exact precedence must be treated as a provisional tie-break
that step 2 reopens, not as settled satisfaction semantics.
close_reason: Step 1 landed in PR #394 (squash-merged 2026-07-26). resolveNodeLabels replaces exact LabelSetKey lookup with satisfaction: exact match wins, then proper-superset satisfying set of size 1 resolves, 0 -> ErrUnknownLabel with split diagnostics, >=2 -> new ErrAmbiguousLabel sentinel. Strictly widening; no representation, edge, or codegen change. Reviewer mutation-tested every guard. Steps 2 and 3 continue as gqlc-h9n.22 (plural satisfaction + property intersection + ADR on exact-match precedence) and gqlc-h9n.23 (multi-label edge types, dead today because endpointLabels returns a single key).

title: test: ISO GQL graph-type schema corpus + coverage gate (foundation for the epic)
description:
Owner direction (2026-07-25): *"first build our own huge dataset of valid ISO GQL
schema files and then merge that in and incrementally increase coverage to 100%
over that as a test suite. this follows a /tdd flow."*

This bead lands the dataset and the gate. It is the **first** bead in the epic:
every sibling then becomes "move these N corpus entries from unsupported to
supported", which is a red-green cycle with a pre-written red.

## Why a corpus rather than per-bug tests

Three separate silent-drop/silent-reinterpret defects (gqlc-uhb, gqlc-h9n.1,
gqlc-h9n.3) share one shape: a grammar alternative the listener neither handles
nor rejects. Per-bug regression tests would have caught none of them, because
nobody knew to write them. A corpus enumerated from the grammar rather than from
known bugs is what makes the unknown-unknowns visible, and a coverage number is
what makes progress against them legible.

## Build on the existing harness, do not replace it

`internal/schema/gql/parser_test.go` already has the right skeleton:

- `test/data/schema/gql/valid/*.gql` + paired `.golden.json`, regenerated with
  `-update` (parser_test.go:41-65)
- `test/data/schema/gql/invalid/*.gql` + the `invalidFixtures` map pinning each to
  a sentinel (parser_test.go:234-272)
- `TestSentinelReachability` (parser_test.go:295) — a bidirectional sweep proving
  every sentinel has a fixture and every fixture maps to a canonical sentinel

The corpus is a scaled-up third category plus one new invariant, reusing all of
the above.

## Corpus shape

One file per grammar alternative or semantic case, systematically enumerated from
GQL.g4 §18.1-18.10 (`nestedGraphTypeSpecification` and everything reachable from
it) and §12.6 (`graphTypeSource`). Minimal files — each isolates one construct, so
a failure names the construct.

Every entry carries a manifest record. Proposed fields:

- **outcome** — `resolves` (a golden exists) or `unsupported` (a sentinel is
  named). No third value, and no entry may be absent from the manifest.
- **feature** — the Annex D feature ID where one applies (GG01-GG05, GG20-GG26,
  GH02, GV50, GC01-GC05), or `mandatory` for constructs with no ID. See the
  `iso-gql-annex-d-optional-features` bd memory.
- **bead** — for `unsupported` entries, the bead that will make it resolve, or an
  explicit `wontfix` pointing at the ADR section justifying the refusal.
- **reason** — one line, for `unsupported` only.

Keep the manifest in Go beside the test rather than in a data file, so a stale
entry is a compile error and the sentinel is a real `error` value, not a string
to be matched.

## The invariant that closes the hole

Beyond the existing sentinel sweep, add: **no corpus entry may parse successfully
into an empty or partial schema.** Concretely, for every entry the parse must
either

- return an error that `errors.Is` the manifest's named sentinel, or
- return a schema equal to the golden,

and **never** return a nil error with a schema that has fewer element types than
the source declares. That last clause is the direct guard against silent drop, and
it is what all three known defects would have failed.

Assert the manifest is exhaustive in both directions, mirroring
`TestSentinelReachability`: a corpus file with no manifest entry fails, and a
manifest entry with no corpus file fails. Without that, adding a `.gql` file
without classifying it re-opens the hole the corpus exists to close.

## Coverage as a number

Report supported / total, and pin the current count with a constant that must be
updated deliberately. A change that moves an entry from `unsupported` to
`resolves` must bump it; a change that regresses one fails. That makes "increase
coverage to 100%" a mechanically checkable claim rather than a narrative one, and
gives each sibling bead an objective done condition.

## Derived from the grammar, not hand-listed

A hand-maintained list drifts exactly the way the listener did. The enumeration
must be checkable against the `.g4` — either generated from it, or verified by a
test that walks the generated parser's rule/alternative metadata and asserts every
alternative reachable from `nestedGraphTypeSpecification` and `graphTypeSource`
appears in the manifest. The second is likely cheaper and is sufficient: it makes
a *new* grammar alternative fail the build until classified.

## Scope boundary

Graph-type DDL only. The query-side corpus is the vendored openCypher TCK
(`test/data/query/cypher/tck`, `just fetch-tck`) and is out of scope here, with one
exception already known to matter: label-expression satisfaction (gqlc-h9n.7) is
where a schema corpus and a query corpus meet, so the corpus must include
multi-label node types even though nothing in DDL alone exercises them.
acceptance_criteria:
A corpus under test/data/schema/gql enumerates one minimal file per grammar alternative reachable from nestedGraphTypeSpecification and graphTypeSource, plus the semantic cases each alternative admits.
Every corpus file has a manifest record declaring outcome (resolves|unsupported), Annex D feature ID or 'mandatory', the bead that will fix it or an explicit wontfix, and a one-line reason.
The manifest is exhaustive in both directions: a corpus file without a manifest entry fails, and a manifest entry without a file fails.
No corpus entry may parse to a nil error with fewer element types than its source declares — the direct silent-drop guard.
All three known defects (gqlc-uhb, gqlc-h9n.1, gqlc-h9n.3) are represented and fail before their fixes land.
A test derived from the generated parser's rule metadata fails when a grammar alternative reachable from the graph-type rules has no manifest entry.
Coverage is reported as supported/total and pinned by a constant that must be updated deliberately; a regression fails.
The corpus lands green — everything unsupported is classified, nothing is silently skipped.
close_reason: Landed in PR #392 (squash 6d4ac8f). 86-file ISO GQL graph-schema corpus plus the three-set coverage gate: rules 133/133, tokens 133/133, alternatives 46/46 with connectorUndirected#1 exempt as unreachable under ALL(*).

comments.text:
# gqlc-h9n.2 — ISO GQL graph-type schema corpus + coverage gate

## Why this exists

`gqlc` generates typed Go from an ISO GQL graph-type schema. Triage on 2026-07-24/25
found three defects with one shape: a **grammar alternative the listener neither
handles nor rejects**. The file parses, the walk collects nothing, `resolve()`
returns an empty schema with a **nil error**, and the eventual diagnostic lands on
the user's *query* file (`unknown label: Person`). The user hit exactly that while
dogfooding.

Known instances: phrase-form element type declarations (`gqlc-uhb`), `COPY OF`
graph type source (`gqlc-h9n.1`), and `UNDIRECTED` edge kind silently reinterpreted
as directed (`gqlc-h9n.3`).

Per-bug regression tests would have caught **none** of them, because nobody knew to
write them. Owner direction, 2026-07-25:

> "first build our own huge dataset of valid ISO GQL schema files and then merge
> that in and incrementally increase coverage to 100% over that as a test suite.
> this follows a /tdd flow."

and, 2026-07-24:

> "we should be able to accept any valid ISO GQL. we should not have our own GQLC
> flavour of ISO GQL."

So this bead lands **a corpus enumerated from the grammar, not from known bugs**,
plus a gate that makes an unclassified grammar branch a build failure. Every sibling
bead in the epic then reduces to "move these N corpus entries from `unsupported` to
`resolves`" — a red-green cycle whose red is already written.

## Working location

Worktree: `/home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc-h9n2-corpus`
Branch: `gqlc-h9n2-schema-corpus` (off `origin/master` at `e510f4b`)

Do **all** work there. Never touch `/home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc` — that
checkout is shared and other sessions switch its branch without warning.

## What already exists (build on it, do not replace it)

`internal/schema/gql/parser_test.go`:

- `fixtureDir = "../../../test/data/schema/gql"`
- `TestValid` (41-65) globs `valid/*.gql`, compares `.golden.json`, `-update` regenerates
- `TestInvalid` (234-253) + `invalidFixtures` (258-272) pin 13 files to sentinels
- `TestSentinelReachability` (295-314) — bidirectional sweep: every sentinel has a
  fixture, every fixture maps to a canonical sentinel

The corpus is a **third category** plus new invariants, reusing this style. Leave
`valid/`, `invalid/`, and the existing tests alone.

`internal/schema/gql/parser.go` shows the parse setup: `gen.NewGQLLexer` →
`antlr.NewCommonTokenStream` → `gen.NewGQLParser` → `gp.GqlProgram()`. `Parse()`
does **not** expose the tree; the corpus test does its own parse, which is
deliberate — the coverage measurement must be independent of the listener under test.

Schema model (`internal/schema/schema.go`): `Schema{Name string, Nodes
map[graph.LabelSetKey]NodeType, Edges map[EdgeKey]EdgeType}`. Note both are **maps
keyed by identity**, so two identical declarations collapse.

## Design — decided, not up for redesign

### 1. Corpus layout

```
test/data/schema/gql/corpus/<clause>/<name>.gql
```

`<clause>` from the section comments in `internal/grammar/gql/GQL.g4`:
`12.6-graph-type-statement`, `17-references`, `18.1-nested-graph-type`,
`18.2-node-type`, `18.3-edge-type`, `18.4-label-set`, `18.5-property-types`,
`18.6-property-type`, `18.7-property-value-type`, `18.8-binding-table-type`,
`18.9-value-type`, `18.10-field-type`.

**Every corpus file is syntactically valid ISO GQL.** A corpus file that produces a
syntax error is a test failure, full stop — the corpus is "valid ISO GQL we do or do
not yet support", so the two outcomes are about the *semantic* stage only. Syntax
negatives stay in the existing `invalid/` dir.

Files are **minimal**: one construct each, so a failure names the construct.
No goldens by default (see §5).

### 2. Manifest — in Go, beside the test

`internal/schema/gql/corpus_test.go`, package `gql`, so sentinels are real `error`
values and a stale entry is a compile error.

```go
type corpusEntry struct {
    file     string // path under corpus/, e.g. "18.2-node-type/phrase_bare.gql"
    outcome  outcome // resolves | unsupported
    sentinel error  // required iff outcome == unsupported, else nil
    feature  string // Annex D ID (GG01.., GH02, GV50, GC01..) or "mandatory"
    bead     string // unsupported only: the bead that will fix it, or "wontfix"
    reason   string // unsupported only: one line
}
```

`outcome` is a defined type with exactly two values. No third value, no default.

There is **no `covers` field**. Coverage is *measured* from the parse tree (§3), not
declared — a declared list drifts exactly the way the listener did.

**Bidirectional exhaustiveness**, mirroring `TestSentinelReachability`: a `.gql` file
under `corpus/` with no manifest entry fails; a manifest entry with no file fails.
Without this, dropping in a file without classifying it re-opens the hole.

### 3. The coverage invariant

Two mechanically derived obligation sets, both required to be fully covered:

**(a) Reachable parser rules.** Scan `internal/grammar/gql/GQL.g4` (relative path
from the test, same as `fixtureDir`). Build rule → referenced-rules. Compute the
transitive closure from roots:

```
createGraphTypeStatement, graphTypeSource, nestedGraphTypeSpecification
```

**Frontier cuts** — stop descending into these, but the rule itself is still
required to be covered:

| Rule | Why cut |
|---|---|
| `graphExpression` | `graphTypeLikeGraph : LIKE graphExpression` drags in the entire query/expression grammar (545 of 574 rules). Query surface is out of scope; it has its own corpus, the vendored openCypher TCK. |
| `nonReservedWords` | `regularIdentifier : REGULAR_IDENTIFIER \| nonReservedWords` — ~200 keyword tokens usable as identifiers. Identifier lexis, not a schema construct. One corpus file using a non-reserved word as an identifier discharges it. |

Because a frontier rule must still be *entered* by some corpus file, a cut that
stops being reachable becomes a coverage failure rather than dead weight. Do not add
a third cut without messaging team-lead with evidence.

**Ground truth, already computed** (verify it, do not take it on faith): with those
two roots plus `createGraphTypeStatement` and those two cuts, the closure is
**133 rules** and **133 tokens**.

**(b) Reachable tokens.** Every token name referenced in the body of a
**non-frontier** reachable rule. 133 of them, all real schema keywords or
punctuation — `DIRECTED`, `UNDIRECTED`, `IMPLIES`, `COPY`, `LIKE`, `BYTES`,
`ZONED`, `VARBINARY`, `RECORD`, `NOTHING`, `SUBSTITUTED_PARAMETER_REFERENCE`, …

**Measurement.** Walk each corpus file's parse tree with a custom
`antlr.ParseTreeListener` recording `ctx.GetRuleIndex()` in `EnterEveryRule` and
`node.GetSymbol().GetTokenType()` in `VisitTerminal`. Map indices to names via the
parser's `RuleNames` / `SymbolicNames`. Union across all corpus files = covered set.
This is generic — no per-rule code, and it cannot drift from the grammar.

**The gate.** `required \ covered` must be empty, for both rules and tokens. The
failure message lists what is uncovered, so it doubles as the authoring worklist.

**No exemptions in this landing.** If you believe a token or rule is genuinely
unreachable inside a valid `CREATE GRAPH TYPE`, message team-lead with the grammar
path that proves it. Do not invent an allowlist — that is the exact mechanism by
which this gate would rot.

Scanner details that matter: strip `//` and `/* */` comments; strip single-quoted
literals; strip `# AltLabel` alternative labels; strip element labels (`name=rule`);
lowercase-initial identifiers are rule refs, uppercase-initial are tokens. Rule
blocks are `^name$` followed by body lines up to a lone `;`. A working Python
prototype of exactly this lives at `/tmp/reach.py` — read it, it is 50 lines and it
produced the 133/133 numbers. Port it, do not re-derive it.

### 4. Silent-drop guard

The direct assertion against the defect class that motivated the bead. For every
`resolves` entry: count `elementTypeSpecification` rule contexts in the tree (same
walk, independent of the listener) and require

```
len(s.Nodes) + len(s.Edges) == that count
```

Exact equality, not `>=`. Minimal one-construct files declare distinct identities so
they never collapse; if you find yourself wanting an exception, the file is wrong.
Note an edge needs its endpoint node types declared too, so an edge file is normally
3 element type specifications → 2 nodes + 1 edge.

For every `unsupported` entry: `Parse` must return the named sentinel with
`errors.Is`. Silence is impossible in either direction.

### 5. Coverage as a pinned number

```go
const (
    wantCorpusEntries   = N
    wantCorpusResolving = M
)
```

Exact equality, both. A change that implements a construct must bump
`wantCorpusResolving`; a regression fails. `t.Logf` the ratio so the number is
visible in CI output. That turns "increase coverage to 100%" into a mechanically
checkable claim and gives every sibling bead an objective done condition.

### 6. Known limitation — state it, do not paper over it

The corpus catches **silent drop** (class 1) and **undocumented rejection**
(class 3). It does **not** catch **silent reinterpretation** (class 2): `UNDIRECTED
EDGE ... CONNECTING (a TO b)` resolves, the element count matches, and the edge is
still recorded as directed. Optional per-entry goldens are the mitigation — add a
`golden bool` field, and for the handful of entries where the *mapping* is the point
(the `gqlc-h9n.3` undirected entry especially) generate a golden that pins today's
**wrong** output, with the `reason` line saying so explicitly and naming the bead
that must change it. A golden capturing a known defect is a good thing here: the
fix's diff then shows the semantic change in review.

Do not silently rely on goldens for correctness of constructs; that is per-bead work.

## Phases (TDD — red before green)

**Phase 1 — harness, red.** Everything in §2/§3/§4/§5 except the corpus itself. Seed
the corpus with a handful of files (you may copy the shapes from the existing
`valid/` fixtures). The coverage test **must fail**, printing the full uncovered
rule and token lists. Save that list to `/tmp/h9n2-uncovered.txt` — it is the
authoring worklist for phase 2. Everything else must pass.

**Phase 2 — corpus, green.** Authored by parallel corpus-author agents, area by
area, each adding `.gql` files plus a Go file declaring
`var corpusArea<X> = []corpusEntry{...}` which the main manifest concatenates. Keep
the per-area split so parallel authors never touch the same Go file.

**Phase 3 — integrate.** Pin the constants, final `just test`, `just lint`,
`just fmt-check`. Note in `internal/schema/gql/corpus_test.go`'s package-level doc
comment what the corpus is and what the two coverage numbers mean.

Phase 1 is yours (carmack). Do it now, get it reviewed, then team-lead fans out
phase 2.

## Non-negotiables

- **Test-first.** Red, then green. The uncovered list *is* the red.
- **Independently mergeable.** If only this PR landed and every sibling bead were
  deferred, `just test` must still pass. So the corpus lands **green**: everything
  not yet supported is classified `unsupported` with a sentinel and a bead.
- **`bd` for task tracking**, never TodoWrite / markdown TODO lists. Do not run
  `bd edit` (opens `$EDITOR`, blocks).
- **Comments state non-obvious constraints only.** No aspirational or justificatory
  commentary, no restating what the code does. Look at the existing comments in
  `schema.go` and `parser.go` for the bar.
- **No AI attribution.** No `Co-Authored-By: Claude` trailer (a commit-msg hook
  rejects it), no "Generated with Claude Code" footer.
- **Never skip hooks** (`--no-verify`, `--no-gpg-sign`).
- Scratch probes go in `/tmp`, never a transient `_test.go` in the tree.
- Quality gates: `just test`, `just lint`, `just fmt-check`, `just tidy-check`.

comments.text:
Phase 1 review round 1 (linus audit) — items 2 and 4 implemented, commit d6a48a6.

Item 2 (real bug in 4acdfab): the silent-drop guard counted every elementTypeSpecification context regardless of nesting depth. closedGraphReferenceValueType (GQL.g4:1926) admits a whole nestedGraphTypeSpecification as a property value type, so the rule recurs. Verified: '(:A { p :: GRAPH { (:B) } })' counted 2 for one node type, and 4 with an edge nested inside — the guard would have failed a correct implementation. Now counts only contexts one nested specification deep, with TestCoverageElementCount pinning the instrument (7 cases incl. twice-nested).

Item 3 reconciled: rather than forbidding zero-element sources outright, the guard reads off the same walk whether the source declares elements inline. COPY OF and LIKE do not, so they must resolve to a NON-EMPTY model; inline sources get the exact count equality. This closes the vacuous 0 == 0 hole and still survives the day COPY OF is implemented.

Item 4 (documented + made self-detecting): 'CREATE GRAPH TYPE t AS COPY OF other' has zero syntax errors but enters createGraphTypeStatement zero times — graphSource : AS COPY OF graphExpression (GQL.g4:331) matches it as createGraphStatement (GQL.g4:313). Rather than only documenting it, measureCoverage now requires every corpus file to enter createGraphTypeStatement, so a file that parses as some other statement fails loudly instead of passing every assertion while exercising nothing.

Correction to the audit: 'COPY OF $src' was listed as verified working; it is a SYNTAX ERROR. SUBSTITUTED_PARAMETER_REFERENCE is DOUBLE_DOLLAR_SIGN PARAMETER_NAME (GQL.g4:3604), so the spelling is $$src. '$src' lexes as GENERAL_PARAMETER_REFERENCE. Matters because that token is one of the 133 and referenceParameterSpecification (GQL.g4:1477) is its only path.

Item 5 (alternative obligation set, 17 uncoverable grammar alternatives) routed to team-lead as a scope call — it expands the phase-1 contract the parallel phase-2 authors build against.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Two corrections and one verification before Phase 2 fan-out (team-lead, 2026-07-25).

AREA SPLIT VERIFIED COMPLETE AND DISJOINT (/tmp/areacheck.py)
  Cross-checked /tmp/h9n2-areas.md against the derived obligation: 0 unassigned
  rules, 0 unassigned tokens, 0 assigned-but-not-required rules. Rule counts sum
  exactly: A 36 + B 17 + C 29 + D1 29 + D2 22 = 133. All 133 tokens assigned to
  exactly one area. This mattered because an unassigned obligation would leave the
  coverage gate red with no author responsible for it.
  Load is uneven — D1 carries 64 of the 133 tokens (scalar type keywords), A carries
  36 of the 133 rules.

AMENDMENT A1.2 CORRECTED — it contradicted A2
  A1.2 gave the AS-prefixed spelling 'CREATE GRAPH TYPE t AS COPY OF other' a corpus
  entry with sentinel ErrNoGraphType. A2 requires every corpus file to enter
  createGraphTypeStatement at least once. That file enters it zero times by
  construction, and ErrNoGraphType is precisely the sentinel for zero times, so the
  two items are mutually exclusive. Both were written in the same amendment.
  Resolution: A2 stands with zero exceptions — no exemption field, no allowlist, no
  per-entry flag, because an exception mechanism in the one invariant designed to
  catch files that silently cover nothing is self-defeating. The AS-prefixed case
  becomes invalid/as_copy_of_graph_type.gql mapped to ErrNoGraphType.
  It belongs there on the merits, not for convenience: it discharges no corpus
  obligation. Its tree holds createGraphStatement, graphSource and graphExpression,
  none of which are in the required-133; the only required symbols it touches are
  the tokens CREATE GRAPH TYPE AS COPY OF, all covered many times over by real
  area-A files.
  Consequence to remember: ErrNoGraphType is the one sentinel no corpus entry may
  ever pin.

AUTHORING GRANULARITY RULED
  'One construct per file' is about isolating failures, not maximising file count.
  Different outcomes must be different files, since outcome is per file. Within one
  outcome, split where a failure stops being informative. For D1 specifically:
  group supported scalar spellings by type family as several properties on one node
  type, and give each unsupported spelling its own file so it is individually
  flippable as the epic progresses. Safe for the silent-drop guard, which counts
  element type declarations rather than properties — forty properties on one node
  type is still one element type and one node.
