title: test(schema): gate resolving-path incidental carriers, not just parse-time ones
description:
Found 2026-07-26 by the gqlc-h9n.17 non-vacuity check, which is the best kind of
finding: the new gate was run against the two historical orphans it was meant to
prevent, reproduced one, and did NOT reproduce the other.

## The two carriage classes

`gqlc-h9n.17` gates **parse-time** incidental carriage: a grammar name that the
whole corpus reaches but that no file in the *owning* area reaches. Verified by
replay at `0b000c60` (parent of the TIMESTAMP fix), where it correctly reports
`localdatetimeType#2 (alt) owned by D1, D2`.

Replayed at `22e02c02` (has the TIMESTAMP fix, lacks the NODE-synonym fix
`7217b180`) it **passes**, i.e. it does not catch the NODE orphan. That is not a
bug in h9n.17. The `NODE` token IS entered at that SHA — by
`18.2-node-type/phrase_form.gql` and `18.9-value-type/constructed_node_closed.gql`
— so parse coverage is genuinely satisfied. But **both of those files are
`unsupported`**: the listener rejects them after the parse succeeds, so nothing
downstream of the parse tree ever sees the name.

`7217b180`'s own commit message says it exactly: "no *resolving* path exercised
an explicit node synonym in nodeTypePattern".

So there are two distinct classes and we currently gate one:

- **parse-time carriage** — some file's parse tree enters the name. GATED by
  h9n.17.
- **resolving-path carriage** — some file that actually *resolves* enters the
  name. NOT GATED. A name can be carried exclusively by files that are expected
  to fail, and every existing gate stays green.

The second class is strictly the more dangerous one, because "the only files
exercising this construct are ones we reject" is a coverage illusion that reads
as coverage in every report we currently produce.

## Why it was not folded into h9n.17

h9n.17's method spec is written in terms of the coverage gate, which measures
the parse tree. Measuring resolving-path carriage needs a different instrument:
run `Parse` (not just the parser) over every corpus file, keep only the files
whose outcome is `resolves`, and recompute carriage over that subset. That is a
second traversal with different inputs, not a parameter on the existing one.

## Sketch

Plausibly cheap: `carried_resolving(area)` = carriage computed over
`{f in area : outcome(f) == resolves}`, compared against the same
section-derived ownership map h9n.17 already builds. The ownership machinery,
the exemption list, and the orphan-reporting format are all reusable as-is;
only the file filter changes.

Open question worth deciding before implementing: should the obligation set for
the resolving gate be the same grammar closure? A construct we deliberately
reject (see gqlc-h9n.6) can never have a resolving carrier, so the resolving
gate would report it as a permanent orphan. Either the obligation set is
narrowed to resolvable constructs, or every deliberate rejection needs an
exemption — and the second option turns the exemption list into a duplicate of
the sentinel registry. Prefer the first, but measure how many names it moves
before committing to it.

Relates to gqlc-h9n.13 (parse-shape recording promoted from report to gate) and
gqlc-h9n.24 (the manifest cannot express a changed-but-still-resolving model).
All three are the same underlying complaint: our instruments measure the parse
tree, and most of the defects this epic finds live downstream of it.

title: schema/gql: non-power-of-two binary precision (INT(7)) silently widens to machine int — decide and record
description:
Noticed 2026-07-26 while ratifying the gqlc-h9n.16 width fold. Not a blocker for
that bead — this behaviour is byte-identical before and after the fold — but the
fold makes the question unavoidable, so record the answer rather than inherit it.

## The question

`GQL.g4:1801` is `INT (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)? notNull?`, under
`binaryExactNumericType`. Precision there is a **bit width** (that is what
separates `binaryExactNumericType` from `decimalExactNumericType`, whose
precision pairs with a `scale` — GQL.g4:1788 vs 1831).

`INT(8)` has an exact counterpart in the model (`TypeInt8`) and gqlc-h9n.16
folds it. `INT(7)` does not. Today, and after h9n.16, it canonicalises to `INT`
and resolves to `graph.TypeInt` — a machine int. The schema author said seven
bits; the model says sixty-four, silently.

That is precisely what ADR 0002's rationale forbids:

  "Losing signedness and width would force codegen to emit int/uint everywhere
   and discard information the schema author explicitly stated."

So the status quo for non-power-of-two widths contradicts the same sentence that
justifies fixing the power-of-two ones. h9n.16 fixes the half with an exact
model counterpart and leaves the other half exactly as it was.

## Why it was not just fixed inside h9n.16

The obvious fix — reject `INT(7)` with `ErrUnsupportedType` — collides with a
standing project directive: *if it is valid ISO GQL, we should allow it; we do
not get our own gqlc flavour.* `INT(7)` is valid ISO GQL. Narrowing acceptance
to protect model fidelity trades one stated goal against another, and that
trade needs a decision, not an implementer's judgement call at edit time.

## Candidate resolutions

1. **Status quo, recorded.** `INT(7)` -> `TypeInt`. Accepts everything valid;
   loses the stated width. Requires an entry in the gqlc-0ri deviation register
   saying so out loud, and a comment at the fallback in
   `internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go` naming it lossy.
2. **Round up to the next supported width.** `INT(7)` -> `TypeInt8`,
   `INT(10)` -> `TypeInt16`, `INT(24)` -> `TypeInt32`. Representationally safe
   in the sense that the wider type holds every value of the narrower one, and
   loses far less than jumping to 64. BUT it depends on reading precision as a
   *minimum* capacity ("at least p bits") rather than an exact one. Nobody here
   has sourced that from ISO 39075, and gqlc-cfj is an open bead about exactly
   this habit of citing the standard without sourcing it. Do not adopt this
   without a citation.
3. **Reject.** `ErrUnsupportedType` for any precision without an exact model
   counterpart. Maximum fidelity, violates the accept-all-valid-GQL directive.

## What to do

Pick one and write it down. If the answer is (1) — which is the cheapest and
the current behaviour — that is a fine answer, but it has to be *stated*, because
right now a reader of ADR 0002 would reasonably predict (3) and a reader of the
project directive would reasonably predict (1), and nothing in the tree
adjudicates.

Applies equally to `UINT(p)`, `INTEGER(p)`, and `FLOAT(p)` for any p without an
exact counterpart. `DECIMAL(p,s)` is NOT in scope: its precision is decimal
digits, not bits, and it is gqlc-5md's problem.

title: test(schema): the corpus manifest cannot express "resolves to a different right thing now"
description:
Surfaced 2026-07-26 while designing gqlc-h9n.16 (Problem A, the width fold).

## The gap

A corpus entry's `outcome` records whether a file parses, resolves, or is
rejected. It cannot express **"this file resolves to a DIFFERENT right thing
after this change than it did before"**.

Concretely: after the width fold, a file declaring `x :: INTEGER(8)` resolves
before AND after. Outcome is `resolves` in both cases. The manifest is satisfied
by both. But the model it resolves to changes from `TypeInt` to `TypeInt8` —
which is the entire point of the change, and the corpus is blind to it.

This is the same blindness as gqlc-uhb (phrase forms parsed and silently
discarded) seen from the other side. There, a wrong model hid behind a passing
`resolves`. Here, a *newly correct* model hides behind the same passing
`resolves`, so the corpus cannot certify that the fix took effect, and — worse —
could not have caught a regression that silently un-fixed it later.

## Why this is not a duplicate of gqlc-h9n.13

gqlc-h9n.13 promotes **parse-shape** recording from report to gate. Parse shape
is unchanged here: `INTEGER(8)` parses identically before and after the fold.
The divergence is entirely downstream of the parse tree, in normalisation. A
parse-shape gate would not fire.

## Why this is not a duplicate of gqlc-h9n.21

gqlc-h9n.21 asserts the model collision a `semanticCase` *describes*. That is a
mechanism for cases the harness already knows are about model identity. This
bead is about ordinary corpus rows, whose whole contract today is an outcome
string.

## Candidate shapes (not yet decided)

1. An optional `model:` assertion on a corpus row — a small structural
   fingerprint (property name -> resolved type constant) checked when present.
   Cheap; opt-in; only as good as the rows that opt in.
2. A golden model snapshot per corpus file, diffed in CI. Catches everything,
   including changes nobody thought to assert; costs a rebaseline ritual on
   every intentional change, which gqlc-exl already shows is expensive here.
3. Leave the corpus alone and require every normalisation change to carry its
   own pin table (which is what gqlc-h9n.16 Problem A does). Zero machinery;
   relies on author discipline; the failure mode is silent.

Option 3 is the status quo. The bead exists to decide whether that is
deliberate. Record the decision either way — if the answer is "the corpus is a
coverage instrument, not a model-identity instrument", that belongs in writing
next to the manifest, because two beads have now independently expected
otherwise.

title: resolver: plural label satisfaction — property intersection, whole-entity rejection, and the ADR
description:
Step 2 of the gqlc-h9n.7 split. Step 1 makes subset matching work but refuses
any query whose label set is satisfied by two or more declared node types. This
bead makes the plural case resolve.

## The rule

A query label expression resolves to the **set** of declared node types whose
label set is a superset of it (with an exact match winning outright, per step 1).
Where that set is plural:

- a **property** reference resolves to the **intersection** — identical name,
  type and nullability across every member, else `ErrUnknownProperty`;
- a **whole-entity** reference (`RETURN p`) is **rejected**.

The property half is not a new commitment: `unionProperty`
(`internal/resolver/resolve.go:731`) already implements exactly this for
multi-candidate edges, including the type-mismatch case
(`resolve.go:744-746`). Substitute `[]schema.NodeType` for `[]schema.EdgeKey`.
Probed behaviour on the edge lane today:

    match (a:A)-[r:R|S]->(b:B) return r.w      -> OK, INT
    match (a:A)-[r:R|S]->(b:B) return r.only   -> unknown property: missing on union member A-[S]->B
    match (a:A)-[r:R|S]->(b:B) return r.skew   -> unknown property: type differs: property:INT vs property:STRING

## Why whole-entity is rejected rather than unioned

The obvious move is to copy the edge side's synthesised sealed interface
(`type TR interface{ isTR() }` with a `switch rel.Type` dispatch). **It does not
carry over, and this is the crux of the bead.** The edge dispatch is total
because a Neo4j relationship has exactly one type, so `rel.Type` is a single
string. The node analogue would dispatch on `dbtype.Node.Labels`, which is a
**set**, and under the very superset rule this bead introduces one runtime node
can satisfy two declared types at once: a node labelled
`{Person, Employee, Contractor}` conforms to both `Person&Employee` and
`Person&Contractor`. "First match wins" makes the emitted struct depend on map
ordering and there is no honest `default`.

The considered alternative was a per-query **intersection struct** carrying only
the common properties. It is implementable and total (decode the intersection
directly, no dispatch) — it is not blocked, only expensive: a new codegen entity
kind with its own naming rule, decode function and collision check against
schema entity names. It is rejected **for now** on the ADR 0006 argument:
widening a rejected query to an accepted one is non-breaking; replacing an
emitted struct that user code already names is not.

## Ripple — this is the bulk of the work

Pluralising the node lane is unavoidable and drags the edge endpoint lane with
it. `endpointLabels` (`resolve.go:503`) returns one `graph.LabelSetKey` read
from `resolved[v] -> nt.Labels`; `closeEdge`, `edgeCandidates`,
`candidateTypes` and `describeTriedEdges` all consume that single key. So
`scope.nodeTypes` goes from `map[string]schema.NodeType` to a candidate lane
mirroring `edgeCands`.

Counted: 20 `nodeTypes[...]` access sites in non-test code (`scope.go`,
`resolve.go`). 13 are presence-only (`_, ok :=`) and survive untouched. **7 read
the value and must each decide what plural means**: `scope.go:144` (BindNode's
`ErrPartBindingTypeConflict` identity compare), `:654` (`refProjectionType`),
`:807` (`Export`), `:918` (`PropertyUseWitness`), and `resolve.go:972` / `:1057`
/ `:1130` (SET / REMOVE / DELETE property validators) — plus `endpointLabels`.

Once the node lane exposes a set, the endpoint predicate composes cleanly:
"does declared `(:Person&Employee)-[:KNOWS]->(...)` match `(a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(...)`"
is just "is `Person&Employee` in the satisfying set of `{Person}`" — the same
predicate reused. `edgeCandidates` becomes a cross-product over
src-set x labels x tgt-set x orientations. Cost is combinatorial, not
conceptual; schemas are small and `labelDeclared` (`resolve.go:1166`) already
documents naive iteration as a deliberate choice.

## ADR

**This bead carries an ADR; step 1 does not.** The plural decision picks a
permanent shape for the type model and, per ADR 0010, that shape leaks into
generated code users name. ADR 0006's argument — the conservative default is
safe because relaxing later is non-breaking and the reverse is not — decides
this one too, which is why it belongs in the same series. ADR 0006 is 64 lines;
this need not be longer.

Also fold in here: a runtime node labelled `{Person, Employee}` matches the
pattern `(:Person)` and is decoded as the `Person` struct, silently dropping
`employeeId`/`title`. That unsoundness predates this epic and step 1 neither
adds nor removes it, but the ADR is where it gets stated rather than left
implicit.
notes:
## Step-2 caveat from the designer's post-implementation pass (2026-07-26)

Two additions after reviewing the step-1 implementation (`160a4bf`).

**1. Exact precedence is a provisional tie-break, not the satisfaction rule.**
Step 1 resolves an exact `s.Nodes[key]` hit outright and only consults the
superset-satisfying set on a miss. That is correct for step 1 — it preserves
observable behaviour exactly, so the change is strictly widening. But under
ISO 39075 §16.8 **both** an exact type and a superset type satisfy the queried
label set, so precedence *hides* the plural case rather than resolving it.

Step 2 must explicitly reopen it. The hazard is that it is invisible: **no
fixture under `test/data/resolver/{valid,invalid}/schemas/` declares `&` at
all**, so nothing exercises the disagreement. A step-2 implementer who does not
know precedence was provisional will inherit it as settled semantics without
ever seeing a test that questions it. The ADR should record it as a step-1
tie-break and say plainly that step 2 revisits it.

**2. A sharper statement of the soundness hazard than this bead's description
carries.** The description above says a `{Person, Employee}` node decoded as the
`Person` struct silently drops `employeeId`/`title`. That understates it. The
worse direction is a **missing property flowing into a typed field**:

    (:Person        { id, name, email })
    (:Person&Employee { employeeId, title })     -- no email

`MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.email` types `email` as `STRING` from the bare
`Person` type. At runtime that pattern also matches `:Person:Employee` nodes,
which carry no `email` at all. So the generated code has a typed field fed by a
property the matched node may not possess — not an extra field discarded, but a
declared field with nothing behind it.

This **pre-dates the epic** and step 1 neither adds nor removes it. It is
recorded here because it is the strongest argument that plural whole-entity
projection must be *rejected* rather than papered over, and because it is the
kind of thing that reads as a step-2 implementation detail until someone ships
a nil deref.

title: resolver: multi-label edge types are declarable but unreachable from any query spelling
description:
Discovered while designing gqlc-h9n.7; not covered by that bead as written, and
a stricter statement than it makes.

A declared edge type may carry a multi-label label set — `EdgeKey.Label` is a
full `LabelSetKey` and `internal/schema/gql/resolve.go:65` builds it via
`e.labels.Key()`. So `-[:KNOWS&FOLLOWS]->` is a legal declaration.

**There is no query spelling anywhere that reaches it.** Probed against a schema
declaring `EdgeKey{Source:"A" Label:"FOLLOWS&KNOWS" Target:"B"}`:

    match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS]->(b:B) return r.since
        -> RESOLVE ERROR: unknown edge: A-[KNOWS]->B
    match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS:FOLLOWS]->(b:B) return r.since
        -> PARSE ERROR: no viable alternative at input 'match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS:'
    match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS|FOLLOWS]->(b:B) return r.since
        -> RESOLVE ERROR: unknown edge: A-[KNOWS]->B, A-[FOLLOWS]->B

Nodes at least have the `:A:B` conjunction spelling. Edges have nothing: Cypher
edge patterns take `|` as *alternation*, not `:` as conjunction, and
`edgeCandidates` (`internal/resolver/resolve.go:471-487`) hardcodes the
singleton assumption by building `graph.LabelSet{L}.Key()` per label.

So a schema author who writes a multi-label edge type has declared something
**dead** — it parses, it resolves into the schema model, and no query can ever
name it. That is the same silent-wrong-answer shape the gqlc-h9n epic exists to
eliminate, one layer down.

## Fix, and the open question

The resolver half is the same shape as the node fix: replace the exact `Label`
compare with `declared.Label ⊇ queried labels`.

The genuinely open part is the **query surface**, and it should be decided
before implementing: there is no conjunction syntax for edge labels in the
Cypher dialect the parser accepts, so subset matching on `-[r:KNOWS]->` would
mean a bare single label silently selects a multi-label declared type. Decide
whether that is wanted, or whether the honest fix is instead to **reject a
multi-label edge type at schema load** with a named sentinel until a query
spelling exists. The second is cheaper, is consistent with the epic's posture of
converting silent gaps into named ones, and is widenable later.

Note the interaction with gqlc-h9n.7 step 2: if node bindings become plural, the
endpoint components of an edge key become sets too, and that machinery is shared.
Sequence this after that bead or accept duplicated work.

title: schema/gql: assert the model collision a semanticCase describes, not just its spelling
description:
A `semanticCase` records a corpus file that parses, resolves, and is still wrong
because the model has no field for what the parse discarded — `CHAR(4)` resolving
to the same `PropertyType` as bare `CHAR`. Six are declared, citing `gqlc-h9n.16`
or `gqlc-h9n.3`.

As of PR #392 each case pins its **spelling**: `TestCorpusManifest` requires the
named file to still contain `"CHAR(4)"`, so the construct cannot be edited out
from under a row that still claims it. That closed the hole where gutting
`scalar_char_fixed_length.gql` left the whole package green at 133/133, 133/133,
46/46.

What is still unpinned is the **collision itself** — that the two spellings really
do resolve to the same model. Nothing in the tree asserts it. If `PropertyType`
silently gained a width field tomorrow, all six rows would keep passing while
describing a blind spot that had closed, and the PR body would keep citing them as
evidence of a limit that no longer exists.

## Fix

Parse the semantic-case file and its un-annotated sibling and `require.Equal` the
resolved models:

| semantic case | sibling it must currently equal |
|---|---|
| `scalar_char_fixed_length.gql` (`CHAR(4)`) | `scalar_character_string.gql`'s `c_bare :: CHAR` |
| `scalar_decimal_precision_scale.gql` (`DECIMAL(10,2)`) | `scalar_dec_alias.gql` |
| `scalar_string_max_length.gql` (`STRING(5)`) | a bare `STRING` carrier |
| `scalar_string_min_max_length.gql` (`STRING(2, 5)`) | ditto |
| `scalar_varchar_max_length.gql` (`VARCHAR(10)`) | a bare `VARCHAR` carrier |
| `kind_undirected_arc_directed.gql` | the `DIRECTED` spelling of the same arc |

The sibling is not always an existing file and the pairing has to be declared
rather than inferred, so this probably means a `sibling string` field alongside
`spelling`.

## Why the assertion is worth more than it looks

It inverts the signal. Today a semantic case is a promise that something is
broken, checked by nobody. With the equality asserted, **the test fails when the
bead lands** — the model gains its field, the two spellings stop resolving
identically, `require.Equal` goes red, and the case gets deleted. That is the same
red-green shape `wantCorpusResolving` already gives for support progress, applied
to the one class of defect coverage can never see.

Follow-up from PR #392 review (finding Q1-E, fix 2). Fix 1 — the spelling pin —
landed in that PR.

## Amendment (PR #392 review, rev-claims final pass)

The reviewer probed the spelling pin for three routes past it. Route 1 is now
closed in #392; routes 2 and 3 belong here, because both close properly only by
asserting the collision.

1. **Comment satisfies the pin.** `require.Contains` read the whole file, so a
   header quoting `CHAR(4)` stood in for GQL that no longer contained it. **Fixed
   in #392** (`546d6da`): the pin now matches against a lexer-stripped copy, so
   none of GQL's three comment forms can carry a spelling on the code's behalf.
   Mutation-tested 6 cases x 4 variants, 24/24 caught; with the strip reverted,
   18 of the 24 escape.
2. **Degenerate spelling.** `spelling: "A"` on the `CHAR(4)` case passes. Nothing
   requires a spelling to discriminate anything — only that it appears. Asserting
   the collision makes the spelling's job checkable: the sibling pair either
   resolves identically or it does not, regardless of what string was declared.
3. **Delete the case wholesale.** Removing the `semanticCase` row along with the
   entry's `bead`/`reason` is green. So the *count* of declared blind spots is
   self-declared: deleting a semantic case is indistinguishable from never having
   had one. Same class as the corpus-dilution gap — adding a file that covers
   nothing is also unpoliced.

Correctly caught already, and worth not regressing: a `semanticCase` naming an
`unsupported` file. The `wrongModel`/`semanticFiles` `ElementsMatch` rejects it,
because a semantic case must by definition resolve.

title: spec: config-multi-target §8.2 calls three fields distinguishing; only one is
description:
§8.2's prefill paragraph blanks `queries`, `gen.go.out` and `gen.go.package` in
an appended target and calls them "the three that must distinguish it". Only
`gen.go.out` must. The same document's §11 says so in as many words:

  Cross-entry checks beyond output overlap. Shared query directories,
  repeated package names, and repeated schema paths are all legal.

Verified: two entries sharing `queries` and `package` with distinct `out` load
cleanly (2 targets, no error). So the document contradicts itself, and the
false half is the one the implementation comment was copied from — the wording
now also sits in internal/cli/init.go's addPrefill doc comment and in
cli-stage-2.md §3.5, both inherited verbatim from §8.2 on branch 4.

The BEHAVIOUR is right and stays: blank is still the honest prefill for all
three, because a second target usually wants its own query directory and
package even though nothing forces it. Only the justification is wrong — 'must
distinguish' should be 'that a second target normally gives its own', with the
`out` requirement stated separately as the one the loader enforces.

Fix in three places: config-multi-target.md §8.2, cli-stage-2.md §3.5,
init.go's addPrefill comment. Prose only, no code change.

Same class as gqlc-5ta: a merged spec sentence that the branch's own evidence
falsifies.

title: cli: pin the blank-out prompt case in the init wizard
description:
Three independent mutations of the init wizard's `out` handling survive the
suite, all reducing to one untested case: nobody ever types a blank (or
whitespace-only) `out` at the prompt.

Found by the branch-4 review (gqlc-0gb.4), reproduced on a scratch
origin/master clone as well — these are PRE-EXISTING, not a branch-4
regression:

- dropping `validateNonBlank` from `validateOut` (init.go)
- dropping the post-form trim of `Go.Out` (§4.2's trim)
- swapping the two checks inside `validateOut`

The current order is the correct one and worth pinning: `CheckOutAgainst("   ")`
returns nil, while `CheckOutAgainst("")` returns a misleading "contains
graph[0]'s output directory" — so validateNonBlank must run first. Nothing
asserts that today.

Fix: add the blank and whitespace-only rows to the `out` validator's table
test, asserting the non-blank message rather than an overlap message.

title: spec: config-multi-target §4.3's sharing bullet overstates a stable outcome
description:
docs/specs/config-multi-target.md:513-517 says of two targets sharing an
output directory: "Files whose names collide (models.go) end up as the
later target's; the rest coexist, so the directory carries two package
clauses and does not compile. The run itself succeeds."

The first and last clauses hold. The middle one ("the rest coexist")
is true on odd runs only. Reproduced 2026-07-25 against
feat/pipeline-multi-target tip with entry 0 out: /tmp/shareprobe2/shared
(absolute) and entry 1 out: shared (relative), five consecutive runs,
exit=0 every time:

  run 1: db.go models.go querier.go invoices.cypher.go -> invoicedb
         people.cypher.go -> people          (5 files, two package clauses)
  run 2: 4 files, invoicedb only            (people.cypher.go deleted)
  run 3: 5 files, two package clauses
  run 4: 4 files, invoicedb only
  run 5: 5 files, two package clauses

Mechanism: inspectOutputs computes BOTH targets' wipe lists before
commitOutputs mutates anything, so target 1's wipe list is derived from
the pre-run contents and never contains a file that target 0's commit
created during this run. From a clean tree target 1's list is empty, so
people.cypher.go survives; next run it is in the list, so it is removed.
Period 2.

So the directory's compilability alternates rather than being stably
broken, and a reader following the spec would predict the wrong state
half the time.

CONTEXT.md's "Output directory" entry was corrected in d301828 on
feat/pipeline-multi-target; it now states the invariant (colliding names
are always the later target's, so the earlier target's package is never
intact) and names the alternation for the non-colliding remainder. The
spec bullet still carries the old wording.

Scope: prose only, one bullet. No code change — the behaviour is a
consequence of the two-phase split working as designed (§7), not a bug.
notes: TRAIL CORRECTION: commit d301828 on feat/pipeline-multi-target ends its body with "Filed gqlc-h8q for the spec bullet." That ID was written before the bead was created and is wrong — gqlc-h8q does not exist. This bead, gqlc-5ta, is the one that commit meant. Left uncorrected in git history because amending a pushed commit needs a force-push, which is not taken without explicit instruction.

title: just test-codegen-fence reports stale results from removed sibling worktrees
description:
`just test-codegen-fence` failed in worktree gqlc-0gb-3-pipeline with 12 issues (errcheck 3, gofumpt 3, ireturn 6) — every one reported against a path under `../gqlc-0gb-2-config/test/data/codegen/...`, a sibling worktree that had already been removed from disk. The worktree under test had zero local changes to test/data/codegen.

`.bin/golangci-lint cache clean` made the recipe green (0 issues) with no source change.

Why it matters here: CLAUDE.md mandates a sibling worktree per session, so worktrees are created and removed constantly, and .bin/golangci-lint's cache is per-worktree but keyed on content that survives the directory. An agent hitting this sees a red gate naming files it cannot open and has no signal that the result is stale — the failure is indistinguishable from a real one until you notice the path points outside the tree.

Possible fixes: have the recipe pass --no-cache or an explicit per-worktree GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE, or prune the cache in ensure-golangci. Needs a repro (create worktree, run fence, remove worktree, run fence elsewhere) before picking one — CI wall-time is critical here, so --no-cache is not free.
notes:
## Correction + partial repro attempt, 2026-07-26 (team-lead)

**The description's premise is wrong in one load-bearing detail.** The cache is
NOT per-worktree. `.bin/golangci-lint cache status` reports
`Dir: /home/antranig/.cache/golangci-lint` — one global cache (57 MiB here)
shared by every worktree. `.bin/` holds only the binary. So the mechanism is not
"a per-worktree cache keyed on surviving content"; it is one cache serving
results across worktrees, with the cached issue records still carrying the
absolute paths of whichever worktree first computed them.

That fits the reported symptom exactly: issues named under
`../gqlc-0gb-2-config/test/data/codegen/...` while linting
`gqlc-0gb-3-pipeline`.

It also reframes the fix menu. A per-worktree `GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE` does not
merely isolate — it *discards the cross-worktree reuse that is currently making
the recipe fast*. Given CLAUDE.md mandates a fresh worktree per session, every
session would start cold. Measure that before choosing it.

**Repro attempt that did NOT reproduce, and why it is still informative.** Five
sibling worktrees (`gqlc-h9n2-corpus-{a,b,c,d1,d2}`) plus seven `/tmp/rev-*`
trees were removed this session; `just test-codegen-fence` in a surviving
worktree then reported `0 issues`. So removal alone is not sufficient. The
removed trees' `test/data/codegen` was clean, so the only thing cached under
their paths was "no issues" — there was no stale *issue* record to misreport.

The repro therefore needs a worktree whose `test/data/codegen` has a **real lint
issue** at lint time, removed, then a lint from a sibling. That is the missing
step; note that if the sibling's content is identical the issue is genuinely
present in it too, so the interesting question is what cache key lets a *stale*
result survive a content change — the bead reports `cache clean` going green
with no source change, which means the key is not purely content. Establish the
key before picking a fix.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #396 (squash-merged 2026-07-26). golangci-lint's cache key is content-only for the current module (internal/cache/cache.go:178 rewrites paths to module-relative) while the cached payload's EncodingIssue.Pos.Filename stays absolute (pkg/goanalysis/issue.go:23), so a hit from worktree A was served verbatim to worktree B. Fix exports GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE to a per-worktree .bin/golangci-cache in the justfile and moves the CI actions/cache path to match; both halves must land together or CI silently runs cold forever.

Reviewer reproduced the bug under an isolated cache (removed tree-A, linted tree-B, got 4 issues all pathed ../tree-A/ plus missing-file warnings, including contamination of an unrelated init.go) and confirmed the fix. Costs measured: cold 78.4s local, warm 0.6s, 20 MiB per warm worktree. git worktree remove without --force still exits 0 because .bin/ is gitignored.

Scope note the reviewer added: CI runners are ephemeral and codegen-fence has no cache step, so this defect was local-workflow-only and never manifested in CI. Observed one-time CI transition cost on #396 itself: lint took 4m56s against a 47s-1m2s baseline, because the restore-key hit an entry saved from the old ~/.cache/golangci-lint path. Steady state is being verified on the next PR.

Follow-up filed as gqlc-b63: nothing in the tree enforces the justfile/ci.yml path coupling.

title: test(schema): pin the three inert measurement guards in the coverage harness
description:
A mutation sweep over the coverage harness' measurement guards found that some are
**inert, not absent**: mutating them changes nothing, because no input in today's nine-file
seed corpus exercises the condition they guard. They are correct code with no test
distinguishing them from a no-op — the class the fabricated-token guard belonged to before
ee53078 pinned it.

Baseline: `TestCorpusGrammarCoverage` red at `rules 78/133, tokens 32/133, alternatives
17/46`, every other test green. Detector: a mutation that moves the gate's reported
coverage while every test keeps its baseline verdict is an unguarded inflation hole.

Sweep script: `/tmp/carm-guardsweep2.sh`. **Use that one, not `/tmp/carm-guardsweep.sh`** —
the first pass was wrong twice and its results should not be quoted. See "sweep method"
below.

## Result

| Guard | Site | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `VisitErrorNode` no-op | `corpus_coverage_test.go:166` | PINNED by `TestFabricatedTokenDoesNotScore` |
| `elementTypes` counts depth 1 only | `corpus_coverage_test.go:97` | PINNED by `TestCoverageElementCount` (nested cases) |
| `declaresElements` fires at depth 0 only | `corpus_coverage_test.go:101` | PINNED by `TestCoverageElementCount` |
| `nestingDepth` counts `nestedSpecRule` | `corpus_coverage_test.go:135` | PINNED by `TestCoverageElementCount` + `TestCorpusOutcomes` |
| `children` blanks error nodes so they contribute no name to attribution | `corpus_coverage_test.go:111-125` | **INERT** |
| `measureCoverage` requires the file to be syntactically valid | `corpus_coverage_test.go:257` | **INERT** — see caveat |
| `stolenBy` joins the required set | `corpus_grammar_test.go:394-396` | **INERT** — needs a seam |

## The three that are open

**`children` blanks error nodes — the one real hole.** This is the attribution half of the
error-recovery defence; `VisitErrorNode` is the token half and is pinned. Removing the
blanking lets a tree built by error recovery match a plausible alternative and score it.
`TestFabricatedTokenDoesNotScore` already feeds a broken source (`CREATE GRAPH TYPE t {
(:A)`, `corpus_test.go:374`) through the `walkCoverage(t, src)` seam, but that particular
recovery shape does not shift any child sequence far enough to steal an alternative. The
pin is therefore: find a broken source whose recovery *does* change attribution, and assert
the alternative is not scored. Finding that source is most of the work, and if no such
source exists the guard is unnecessary — either outcome is worth knowing.

**`measureCoverage` requires syntactic validity.** Inert because no seed file is broken,
and it is not really a measurement guard — it is a fail-fast assertion aimed at corpus
authors, whose "test" is that a broken corpus file fails loudly. Pinning it properly means
asserting that a `require` fires, which needs either a fake `*testing.T` or extracting the
check into a pure function. Low value, non-trivial cost; decide whether it is worth it
before doing it.

**`stolenBy` joins the required set.** Inert because today's only thief is itself a
candidate, so the append is a no-op — `corpus_grammar_test.go:390-392` already says so.
Pinning needs a seam first: `requiredAlternatives` reads package-level
`alternativeExemptions` directly, so an exemption whose `stolenBy` is not a candidate
cannot be injected. Parameterise it, or split out a pure helper.

## Sweep method — two mistakes worth not repeating

**1. Do not run a `-run` subset.** The first pass used `-run
'TestCorpus|TestAlternative|TestExemption|TestFabricated|TestGrammar|TestObligation'`,
which silently excluded `TestCoverageElementCount` — the *only* test that feeds the
collector a nested element type, and therefore the only test that can see either depth
guard. Three guards were reported inert that are in fact pinned. A sweep that decides
whether a guard is tested must run every test.

**2. Prefer a mutation that relocates a guard over one that widens it.** Widening
`declaresElements`' depth check from `== 0` to `>= 0` is an *equivalent mutant*: the field
is a bool that saturates, and a depth-0 `nestedSpec` exists whenever any nested one does,
so no input can distinguish the two. Relocating it to `== 1` fails four tests immediately.
A widening mutation on a saturating value proves nothing.

## Do not

Do not pin any of these by adding a file to `test/data/schema/gql/invalid/` or a seed
corpus file. They must be tested through the corpus-independent `walkCoverage(t, src)` seam
(`corpus_coverage_test.go:233`), so the tests stay independent of what any corpus author
does — and each guard's own inertness proves no such fixture exists today.
notes:
RESOLVED (pending commit) 2026-07-25: the 'children blanks error nodes' guard is NOT inert, it is load-bearing, and there is now a witness.

Probe /tmp/h9n2probe/carmerr reimplements children() twice over the same tree (error nodes blanked vs named) and reports every rule whose child sequence differs. 21 of 33 broken sources differ somewhere. The dangerous class is ANTLR's single-token INSERTION: the error node's token type is exactly the one the alternative wanted, so the unblanked sequence can be a perfect match for an alternative the input never took. Substitution and deletion recoveries are harmless because the resulting sequence matches nothing.

Witness: CREATE GRAPH TYPE t { (:A), (:B), (:A)-[:R]->(:B }

Recovery invents the closing RIGHT_PAREN, leaving destinationNodeTypeReference with children LEFT_PAREN nodeTypeFiller RIGHT_PAREN — exactly its alternative 2 (GQL.g4:1623-1626), which is REQUIRED and on the authors' worklist. Removing the blanking scores destinationNodeTypeReference#2 from a file that does not parse.

Pinned by TestFabricatedTokenDoesNotAttribute in corpus_test.go, mutation-verified: passes as-is, fails on 'Should be false / the recovered endpoint must not score' when the ErrorNode case is dropped from children(). TestFabricatedTokenDoesNotScore still passes under that same mutation, which confirms the two guards are independent — as the comment at corpus_test.go:369-372 already claimed.

Why earlier candidates were all false leads: arcTypePointingRight and nestedGraphTypeSpecification also show a sequence diff, but both are SINGLE-alternative rules, and alternativeIndex.tag returns early for those, so nothing about them is ever attributed. A sequence diff is necessary but not sufficient; the rule must be multi-alternative AND the unblanked sequence must match one of its alternatives.

Remaining on this bead: measureCoverage's syntactic-validity require (low value, needs a fake *testing.T) and stolenBy joining required (needs a seam).
COMMITTED 4c9ff26 (2026-07-25). The children/error-node blanking guard is now pinned by TestFabricatedTokenDoesNotAttribute. One of the three items on this bead is discharged; the two that remain are measureCoverage's syntactic-validity require (needs a fake *testing.T or a pure-function extraction; low value) and stolenBy joining required (needs a seam in requiredAlternatives).

title: schema/gql: source Annex D conformance feature ids, or stop citing them
description:
The corpus `corpusEntry.feature` field is documented as "the ISO GQL Annex D conformance feature id, or `mandatory`". Its purpose is narrow and it is only load-bearing on `unsupported` entries: for a construct we decline, the *only* thing that makes declining conformant is that construct being an Annex D **optional** feature. On a `resolves` entry the field carries no weight, because we support the construct either way.

The problem is that on exactly the entries where the field matters, we cannot currently source it. There is no Annex D material anywhere in the repo (checked `docs/specs`, `docs/adr`, the grammar, 2026-07-25), and the ids that reached the tree were written from memory:

- `internal/schema/gql/corpus_area_a_test.go` carried `feature: "GG02"` on `12.6-graph-type-statement/like_graph.gql`, with a reason string that claimed "conformant because GG02 is an optional Annex D feature". That is an unsourced id being used to discharge a conformance claim.
- `/tmp/h9n2-areas.md` carried `GV50` for LIST/ARRAY on the same basis.
- The struct doc comments in `corpus_test.go` and the author brief both use `GG01` / `GV50` as format examples, which teaches the fabrication to five authors.

Note that `"mandatory"` is NOT the safe fallback for a declined construct — it is worse than an unsourced id. If a construct is mandatory then declining it is non-conformant, so `feature: "mandatory"` on an `unsupported` entry asserts a defect rather than excusing one. The two values are not interchangeable and the fallback direction depends on the outcome.

Interim position taken for the corpus PR: no entry cites an Annex D id. Declined constructs record the dependency honestly — that conformance rests on the construct being optional, unsourced — and point here.

This bead closes when either the ids are sourced against the actual standard text and the citing entries carry real ones, or the field is replaced by something we can actually substantiate.
notes:
2026-07-25, team-lead, measured. Two corrections to the description above, both found by
running the harness rather than reasoning about it.

1. THREE entries carried a fabricated id, not one. Full inventory:
     corpus_area_a_test.go:18  like_graph.gql                 GG02  (unsupported)
     corpus_area_c_test.go:16  pattern_undirected.gql         GE03  (unsupported)
     corpus_area_c_test.go:23  kind_undirected_arc_directed   GE03  (resolves)
   I had only catalogued GG02. The other two surfaced from a require.Len failure dump,
   i.e. by accident -- which is the argument for item 2.

2. The description's claim that "mandatory" on an unsupported entry "asserts a defect
   rather than excusing one" is right about the mechanics and wrong about the intent.
   Asserting a defect is EXACTLY what the corpus should do for the phrase forms: the
   repo owner's standing rule is "if it is valid ISO GQL, we should allow it; we should
   not have our own GQLC flavour of ISO GQL", so an unsupported entry for valid ISO GQL
   is a declared conformance gap, and the bead is what closes it. Both edgeTypePhraseFiller
   entries already carry mandatory + gqlc-uhb on exactly that basis and they are correct.

   The sharpened rule, which is what the field should mean:
     - "mandatory"  = declining this is non-conformant. Free on a resolves entry;
                      on an unsupported entry it declares a gap, and the bead closes it.
     - "unsourced"  = we do not know. This is the honest value ONLY for a construct
                      declined PERMANENTLY, because there the claim is "declining this is
                      still conformant" -- precisely the unsourceable one.
   Applied, exactly one entry qualifies as unsourced: like_graph.gql, bead gqlc-0ri,
   permanently declined because LIKE needs live data. Everything else is mandatory.

FIX SHAPE, prototyped and verified in /tmp/goldencheck, diff at /tmp/lead/patch/:
close the class with a mechanism instead of an instruction. featureValues is a closed
set {"mandatory","unsourced"} and TestCorpusManifest does require.Contains against it.
Verified it fires on the real violation:
    []string{"mandatory","unsourced"} does not contain "GG02"
    12.6-graph-type-statement/like_graph.gql: feature must be "mandatory" or "unsourced"

Why a mechanism and not the brief: "do not cite an Annex D id" was a rule with no
mechanism -- A14's exact failure mode -- and it was violated 3 times in 9 entries before
anyone noticed. Worse, the corpusEntry.feature doc comment itself said "(GG01, GV50, ...)",
so the struct was teaching the fabrication it forbade. Five authors were about to read it.

title: schema/gql: mutation-sweep every harness guard, prove each is load-bearing by deletion
description:
The corpus harness is a gate whose only job is to fail when the corpus stops discharging its obligations. Three separate defects this epic (amendments A11, A14, A17) were guards that looked right and asserted nothing: a `required \ covered` difference that is empty when `required` is empty, a constraint written into the brief with no mechanism behind it, and a count pin that cannot observe a membership change.

The general lesson linus drew is stronger than any of the three fixes: **every configuration entry and every assertion must be load-bearing, and the only proof is deletion**. Measured instance: two of the three `coverageRoots` entries were +0 rules / +0 tokens — dead config that looked like the load-bearing part of the closure.

This bead is the systematic version of that check across the whole harness, run once the corpus is complete and the gate is green, because a mutation sweep against a red gate cannot distinguish a kill from the pre-existing failure.

Method, per guard: mutate it so the property it claims to enforce is violated, run the package, and record whether the suite fails and *which* assertion fired. A mutation that leaves the suite green is a guard that is not load-bearing; a mutation that fails at a *different* assertion than the mutated one means the guard is redundant with an earlier check and should say so or go.

Known-suspect classes to cover, not an exhaustive list:
- every count pin (`wantObligationRules`, `wantObligationTokens`, `wantInvisibleAlternatives`, `wantCorpusEntries`, `wantCorpusResolving`) — a count cannot see a compensating pair
- every set-difference assertion — check the empty-`required` case explicitly
- each entry of `coverageRoots` and each cut, deleted individually, with the rule/token delta recorded
- the syntax-validity and attribution checks in `measureCoverage`, whose ordering is what actually makes a fabricated token unscoreable (see the corrected justification for the token-fabrication pin)
- the area-ownership disjointness assertion

title: schema/gql: ground the GH02 undirected-edge and GG04 LIKE rejections in defensible reasons
description:
Two optional features gqlc rejects today with sentinels, whose stated reasons do
not survive scrutiny. Both rejections are probably right; both need a defensible
reason before the ADR (gqlc-0ri) can record them.

## GH02 — undirected edge types (`ErrUndirectedEdge`)

`EnterEdgeTypePatternUndirected` (listener.go:150-152) fails on any
`arcTypeUndirected` (`~[...]~`).

**The reason to avoid.** "An undirected edge cannot be faithfully represented
against a directed-edge store" overstates the case.
`edgeTypePatternUndirected : sourceNodeTypeReference arcTypeUndirected
destinationNodeTypeReference` keeps the endpoint *types* ordered, so a lossy
mapping — canonical stored direction plus undirected matching — is mechanically
available. Rejecting on unrepresentability invites a reviewer to point at that
mapping.

**The reason that holds.** An undirected edge is a **distinct element kind**, not
a directed edge matched in both directions.

CITED — *A Researcher's Digest of GQL* (ICDT 2023; "We follow the formal
definition adapted by the GQL Standard"), Def. 2: a property graph is
`⟨N, Ed, Eu, lab, endpoints, src, tgt, prop⟩` where `Eu` is a **separate** set of
undirected edge ids, `src, tgt : Ed → N`, and `endpoints : Eu → 2^N` with
`|endpoints(e)| ∈ {1,2}` — unordered.

And the distinction is **observable at runtime**, so a lossy mapping is detectably
wrong rather than merely imprecise: `<edge> IS [NOT] DIRECTED` (§19.8) and
`n IS SOURCE OF e` (§19.10) would both answer incorrectly for an undirected edge
stored with a canonical direction. Neo4j has no such element kind — every
relationship has a startNode and an endNode.

Add that GH02 *"Undirected edge patterns"* carries an Annex D feature ID and is
therefore optional, so declining it is conformant.

**Also note this reaches the query side, not just DDL.** GQL distinguishes
`<-[]->` (`fullEdgeLeftOrRight`, directed either way) from `-[]-`
(`fullEdgeAnyDirection`, includes undirected). Cypher's `-[r]-` is GQL's
`<-[]->`, not `-[]-`. Any future GQL query-language support inherits this, so the
ADR should scope the decision to the whole language rather than to graph-type DDL.

## GG04 — graph type `LIKE` a graph (`ErrUnsupportedSource`)

    graphTypeLikeGraph : LIKE graphExpression
    graphExpression    : graphReference | objectExpressionPrimary
                       | objectNameOrBindingVariable | currentGraph

`CURRENT_GRAPH` and binding variables are session state. A static generator has
no session, so `LIKE` is genuinely unresolvable — this reason does hold. Record it
against GG04 *"Graph type like a graph"* and note the contrast with `COPY OF`
(gqlc-h9n.1), whose catalog-path form **is** statically resolvable, so the two
rejections do not share a justification even though they share a sentinel.

Splitting `ErrUnsupportedSource` into two errors is likely worthwhile for exactly
that reason: one says "session state, never resolvable", the other says "resolvable
in principle, blocked by gqlc's one-graph-type rule".
acceptance_criteria:
The undirected-edge rejection is justified by undirected edges being a distinct element kind whose directedness is observable via IS DIRECTED and IS SOURCE OF, plus GH02 optionality — not by an unrepresentability claim.
The LIKE rejection is justified by graphExpression reaching session state, recorded against GG04.
ErrUnsupportedSource is split so that LIKE and COPY OF no longer share one error with two incompatible justifications.
The ADR scopes the undirected decision to the whole language, noting GQL's <-[]-> versus -[]- distinction affects future query support.
Both decisions are pinned by tests naming the specific error.

title: schema/gql: decide GG21 label implication (=>) — implement key label sets or ADR the rejection
description:
`rejectLabelImplication` (listener.go:140-148) fails on any `IMPLIES` token, so
the whole key-label-set-with-implication form is refused:

    nodeTypeKeyLabelSet : labelSetPhrase? IMPLIES     # GQL.g4:1534-1536
    edgeTypeKeyLabelSet : labelSetPhrase? IMPLIES     # GQL.g4:1577-1579

This is optional feature **GG21 "Explicit element type key label sets"**, so
declining it is legitimate under §24.2 minimum conformance. Two things are
nonetheless wrong today.

## 1. The rejection is undocumented and its scope is mislabelled

`ErrLabelImplication` says `label implication ("=>") is not supported`, and the
listener comment calls the accepted form "the plain key label set (`:Label`)".
But per the standard's BNF the part *before* `=>` is the key label set and the
part *after* is implied content — so what gqlc calls "the plain key label set" is
in fact a complete label set with an **inferred** key label set (optional feature
**GG22**). The naming inverts the standard's own vocabulary. Record the rejection
as "GG21 not supported" in the ADR, and fix the vocabulary.

Note `labelSetPhrase?` is optional, so `=> :Thing` with an *empty* key label set
is also grammar-legal and also refused.

## 2. Deciding whether to implement it needs the identity model first

`=>` is the syntax for declaring a key label set explicitly. Without a
key-label-set concept in the model there is nothing for the syntax to populate,
so this bead is blocked on that model change rather than being a listener
addition.

## Vendor semantics diverge — do not pick one by accident

- **Microsoft Fabric**: secondary-label properties "are automatically inherited"
  (property inheritance across declarations).
- **Neo4j** (GA 2026.06): same syntax, called *identifying label* + *implied
  labels*, with **no** property inheritance, and a label may not be both
  identifying and implied — which rules out hierarchies.

Two implementations, same syntax, incompatible semantics. Whether 39075:2024
mandates cross-declaration property inheritance is **UNRESOLVED** and could not
be settled from public sources. Fabric's own conformance table marks GG21 **No**
while its graph-types article uses `=>` and warns the syntax "isn't currently
supported directly for graph" — i.e. `=>` is the standard's syntax, unimplemented
there.

So implementing `=>` means choosing an inheritance semantics that the standard
may not endorse. Under the no-dialect principle that argues for implementing only
the part both vendors agree on — the key label set as identity, with implied
labels contributing to the complete label set — and explicitly *not* implementing
property inheritance until the standard's position is known.
acceptance_criteria:
The rejection or support of => is recorded against feature ID GG21, not as a generic deviation.
The vocabulary is corrected so 'key label set' names the part before => and 'implied content' the part after, matching the standard's BNF.
The empty-key-label-set spelling (=> :Thing) has a decided, tested outcome.
If implemented: implied labels contribute to the complete label set, and property inheritance is explicitly NOT implemented, with the standard's unresolved position recorded.
If rejected: the ADR states GG21 is an optional feature declined pending a resolution of the Fabric/Neo4j inheritance divergence.

title: schema/gql: model the key label set as node type identity, distinct from the complete label set
description:
gqlc's schema model has no key-label-set concept. `internal/graph/labelset.go`
`LabelSet.Key` canonicalises a type's *complete* label set and that string is
then used as the type's identity throughout (`schema.Schema.Nodes` is keyed by
it).

ISO GQL separates three notions (researched 2026-07-25; see the
`gqlc-iso-node-type-identity` bd memory for the full evidence):

| Notion | Feature | Grammar |
|---|---|---|
| element type **name** | GG20 | `nodeTypeName`, `localNodeTypeAlias` |
| **key label set** — identity | GG21/22/23 | the part *before* `=>` |
| **complete** label set | — | the whole `labelSetPhrase` |

`nodeTypeKeyLabelSet : labelSetPhrase? IMPLIES` (GQL.g4:1534) — the standard's
own BNF names the pre-`=>` part the key label set and the post-`=>` part implied
content.

## The evidence that the key label set is identity

Annex D defines **GG25 "Relaxed key label set uniqueness for edge types"**. A
feature that *relaxes* key-label-set uniqueness for edge types establishes that
the base rule is key-label-set uniqueness across element types. CITED at the
level of Annex D feature names, which Ultipa and Microsoft Fabric publish
identically (Fabric's page is reviewed by Stefan Plantikow, a GQL editor).

`ErrDuplicateNodeType` therefore enforces the right *rule* against the wrong
*key*: it dedupes on complete label sets where the standard dedupes on key label
sets.

## Scope

This is the model change, not the `=>` syntax. Even with `=>` still rejected, the
degenerate case matters: when a declaration has no `=>`, its key label set is
inferred (GG22) and merely *coincides* with its complete label set. Representing
that coincidence explicitly is what makes the model correct and makes GG21
implementable later as a syntax addition rather than a model rewrite.

Depends on the satisfaction fix landing first, because changing what identifies a
node type while lookup is still exact-match would change which schemas are
accepted for reasons unrelated to identity.

## Do not import vendor semantics

Fabric says secondary-label properties are "automatically inherited". Neo4j
implements the same construct as identifying + implied labels with **no** property
inheritance, and forbids a label being both. Whether 39075:2024 mandates
cross-declaration property inheritance is **UNRESOLVED**. Model the key label set
without committing to an inheritance rule.
acceptance_criteria:
The schema model represents a node/edge type's key label set separately from its complete label set, including the inferred (no =>) case.
Node and edge type identity and the duplicate-type check key on the key label set, not the complete label set.
Edge endpoint resolution for the inline-filler form matches on the key label set, so an endpoint (:A) resolves against a node type whose key label set is {A} and whose complete label set is larger.

title: schema/gql: LIST / ARRAY property types require a parameterised type model
description:
`valueType` has three list alternatives (GQL.g4:1723-1725), none supported:

    | listValueTypeName LEFT_ANGLE_BRACKET valueType RIGHT_ANGLE_BRACKET (LEFT_BRACKET maxLength RIGHT_BRACKET)? notNull?  #listValueTypeAlt1
    | valueType listValueTypeName (LEFT_BRACKET maxLength RIGHT_BRACKET)? notNull?                                          #listValueTypeAlt2
    | listValueTypeName (LEFT_BRACKET maxLength RIGHT_BRACKET)? notNull?                                                    #listValueTypeAlt3

with `listValueTypeName : LIST | ARRAY` (1968-1975). So `LIST<STRING>`,
`STRING LIST`, `STRING ARRAY`, `LIST` and `ARRAY[10]` are all one type family
spelled five ways. Verified 2026-07-25: `LIST<STRING>` fails with
`ErrUnsupportedType`.

Lists matter more than the other composite types because neo4j property values
are natively list-capable — a homogeneous list of primitives is a *storable
property*, unlike `RECORD` or `PATH`. This is the one composite family that a
property-graph code generator arguably must support.

## The blocker: the type model is string-keyed

`normaliseType` (propertytype.go:110-113) maps a canonicalised *spelling* to a
flat `graph.PropertyType` enum. A list type is parameterised by its element
type, which a flat enum and a string key cannot express. So this bead is not a
table entry — it needs `graph.PropertyType` to gain a composite representation,
and every consumer (Go type rendering, driver value conversion, the resolver's
property type-checking) to handle it.

That makes it the largest single item in the epic and the reason it is filed
separately from the missing scalars.

## Latent bug this activates

`hasNotNull` (propertytype.go:41-46) reports NOT NULL by scanning the whole
subtree for a `NotNullContext`. For `LIST<STRING NOT NULL>` the inner element's
qualifier would be read as the outer list's, so a nullable list of non-null
strings would be modelled as a non-null list. Harmless while lists are rejected;
a correctness bug the moment they are not. The alternatives are labelled
(`#listValueTypeAlt1` etc.), so the outer `notNull?` is directly addressable and
the subtree scan can be replaced with a per-alternative read.

## Alt3 has no element type

`LIST` and `ARRAY` with no `<T>` are legal and mean a list of any value type.
Decide whether that maps to something (`[]any`) or is rejected with a precise
error; it must not fall through to a generic `ErrUnsupportedType`.
acceptance_criteria:
All five list spellings (LIST<T>, T LIST, T ARRAY, bare LIST, ARRAY[n]) resolve or are rejected with a precise error, never a generic ErrUnsupportedType.
graph.PropertyType represents a parameterised list type; Go rendering and driver conversion handle it.
hasNotNull no longer attributes an element type's NOT NULL to the enclosing list.
Nested lists (LIST<LIST<INT>>) have a decided, tested outcome.

title: schema/gql: missing predefined property types — BYTES, TIME, DURATION, SIGNED/UNSIGNED numerics
description:
`typeSpellings` (propertytype.go:53-108) covers boolean, character-string,
numeric, date and timestamp families. Four grammar-reachable predefined-type
families are absent and therefore fail with `ErrUnsupportedType`, even though
each has an unambiguous Go and neo4j mapping.

All four verified rejected 2026-07-25 against a built binary.

## 1. Byte strings — GQL.g4:1760-1763

    byteStringType : BYTES (LEFT_PAREN (minLength COMMA)? maxLength RIGHT_PAREN)? notNull?
                   | BINARY (LEFT_PAREN fixedLength RIGHT_PAREN)? notNull?
                   | VARBINARY (LEFT_PAREN maxLength RIGHT_PAREN)? notNull?

`byteStringType` is listed in `predefinedType` (1743) but has no entry.
Maps to `[]byte`.

## 2. Time-of-day — GQL.g4:1881-1889

    timeType      : ZONED TIME notNull? | TIME WITH TIME ZONE notNull?
    localtimeType : LOCAL TIME notNull? | TIME WITHOUT TIME ZONE notNull?

Both are `temporalInstantType` alternatives (1863-1864) and both are missing,
while their datetime siblings (`ZONED DATETIME`, `LOCAL DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP
WITH/WITHOUT TIME ZONE`) are present. neo4j has native `Time` and `LocalTime`,
so this is an omission rather than a mapping problem.

Note there is no bare `TIME` spelling in the grammar — the zone qualifier is
mandatory — so the four spellings above are the complete set.

## 3. Duration — GQL.g4:1891-1898

    temporalDurationType      : DURATION LEFT_PAREN temporalDurationQualifier RIGHT_PAREN notNull?
    temporalDurationQualifier : YEAR TO MONTH | DAY TO SECOND

The qualifier is mandatory, so exactly two spellings exist. neo4j has a native
`Duration`. Whether the two qualifiers collapse onto one Go type or need
distinguishing is the only real design question here.

## 4. SIGNED / UNSIGNED verbose numerics — GQL.g4:1803, 1816

    signedBinaryExactNumericType   : ... | SIGNED? verboseBinaryExactNumericType
    unsignedBinaryExactNumericType : ... | UNSIGNED verboseBinaryExactNumericType

These are plain aliases for spellings already in the table — `SIGNED INTEGER` is
`INTEGER`, `UNSIGNED INTEGER32` is `UINT32`, and so on across all nine verbose
forms. Both verified reachable and rejected 2026-07-25.

**The comment at propertytype.go:50-52 asserts the opposite** and must be
corrected:

    // Only grammar-reachable spellings appear: e.g. SIGNED, UNSIGNED,
    // NUMERIC, CHARACTER, bare DATETIME/LOCALDATETIME are listed in some
    // references but the GQL grammar does not accept them, so they cannot occur.

`NUMERIC`, `CHARACTER` and the bare `DATETIME`/`LOCALDATETIME` halves of that
claim are correct; the `SIGNED`/`UNSIGNED` half is not.

## Note on canonicalSpelling

`canonicalSpelling` (propertytype.go:118-125) truncates at the first `(`, which
is what makes `DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)` collapse to `DURATION` and lose its
qualifier. Adding duration therefore needs the qualifier read from the tree, not
from the truncated spelling — the string-keyed lookup cannot express it.
acceptance_criteria:
BYTES, BINARY and VARBINARY resolve to a byte-slice property type.
ZONED TIME, TIME WITH TIME ZONE, LOCAL TIME and TIME WITHOUT TIME ZONE resolve to time-of-day property types.
DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH) and DURATION(DAY TO SECOND) resolve, with the qualifier read from the parse tree rather than the truncated spelling.
All nine SIGNED/UNSIGNED verbose numeric spellings resolve to the same types as their non-prefixed equivalents.
The false SIGNED/UNSIGNED unreachability claim in the propertytype.go comment is corrected.
Each new spelling has a test; generated Go and driver conversion handle the new types.
notes:
2026-07-26 (team-lead, while ratifying gqlc-h9n.16): the doc comment on `typeSpellings` (internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go) is FACTUALLY WRONG about this bead's subject. It reads: "SIGNED, UNSIGNED, NUMERIC, CHARACTER, bare DATETIME/LOCALDATETIME are listed in some references but the GQL grammar does not accept them, so they cannot occur."

The grammar does accept SIGNED and UNSIGNED. GQL.g4:1803 is `SIGNED? verboseBinaryExactNumericType` and GQL.g4:1816 is `UNSIGNED verboseBinaryExactNumericType` — where UNSIGNED is MANDATORY, i.e. it is the only spelling of that alternative. Both are real lexer tokens (SIGNED at :3448, UNSIGNED at :3478). So `SIGNED INTEGER8` and `UNSIGNED INTEGER8` parse, canonicalise to "SIGNED INTEGER8" / "UNSIGNED INTEGER8", miss typeSpellings, and return ErrUnsupportedType.

Two consequences. (1) The rejection is honest — ErrUnsupportedType, not a wrong model — so this is a gap, not the accepted-input-nil-error-wrong-model family. (2) The comment's stated REASON for the gap is false, which matters more than the gap: it tells the next reader not to bother looking, and it is exactly the unsourced-universal shape that gqlc-cfj is about. The NUMERIC / CHARACTER / bare-DATETIME half of that sentence has NOT been checked and may well be right.

The gqlc-h9n.16 implementer is rewriting that doc comment and has been told to correct the SIGNED/UNSIGNED clause in passing, without implementing the types. Implementing them stays here.

title: schema/gql: UNDIRECTED edge kind with a directed arc is silently reinterpreted as directed
description:
`edgeTypePattern` (GQL.g4:1553-1555) lets `edgeKind` and the arc direction
disagree:

    edgeTypePattern
        : (edgeKind? edgeSynonym TYPE? edgeTypeName)? (edgeTypePatternDirected | edgeTypePatternUndirected)
        ;
    edgeKind : DIRECTED | UNDIRECTED ;

`EnterEdgeTypePattern` (listener.go:154) never reads `edgeKind` at all. It
branches solely on `EdgeTypePatternDirected()`. So an `UNDIRECTED` keyword in
front of a right-pointing arc is silently discarded and the edge is generated as
directed.

Verified 2026-07-25:

    CREATE GRAPH TYPE G AS {
      NODE TYPE Person (p :Person {id STRING, name STRING}),
      UNDIRECTED EDGE TYPE K (p)-[:KNOWS]->(p)
    }

resolves, and `MATCH (p1:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(p2:Person)` type-checks against it —
i.e. the schema author wrote `UNDIRECTED` and got a directed edge type with no
diagnostic. The mirror case is handled by accident: `DIRECTED EDGE TYPE K
(p)~[:KNOWS]~(p)` is rejected, but with `ErrUndirectedEdge` (because the arc is
undirected), not because the two disagree.

## What to decide

Whether ISO GQL's static semantics make a kind/arc contradiction a syntax rule
violation is a prose question. Two candidate outcomes, both acceptable under the
no-dialect principle:

- the standard forbids the contradiction -> reject it with a new sentinel naming
  both the declared kind and the arc direction;
- the standard permits it and `edgeKind` is redundant with the arc -> say so in
  the ADR and add a test pinning that `UNDIRECTED ... ->` is deliberately read
  as directed.

What is *not* acceptable is the current state, where nothing records which of
those two is intended. Note the interaction with the undirected-edge-type
rejection decision: if undirected edges are rejected outright, the natural
reading is that `UNDIRECTED` in any position must be refused, which makes this
a one-line fix rather than a semantic question.
acceptance_criteria:
edgeKind is read by EnterEdgeTypePattern rather than ignored.
A kind/arc contradiction produces a decided, tested outcome — either a sentinel naming both the declared kind and the arc direction, or a pinned deliberate-acceptance test.
The decision is recorded in the subset ADR.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Resolution guidance, verified 2026-07-25 with an out-of-tree ANTLR probe (linus, gqlc-h9n.2 design audit):

`schema.EdgeType` embeds `EdgeKey{Source,Label,Target}` and has **no undirectedness field** (internal/schema/schema.go:28-40). Probe result: `UNDIRECTED EDGE E (:A)-[:E]->(:B)` and `DIRECTED EDGE E (:A)-[:E]->(:B)` both parse clean and both yield edge `{A E B}` — byte-identical. So a golden test cannot pin this defect at all; there is no discriminating output to capture.

That kills the option of 'fix it by representing undirectedness in a golden' and narrows this bead to two real choices:

(a) Give Schema an undirected representation first, then map the kind onto it. Larger blast radius: EdgeKey identity, resolver, codegen, and the generated Cypher all assume directedness.

(b) **Reject** `edgeKind = UNDIRECTED` in the listener, converting this from class 2 (silent reinterpretation) to class 3 (documented rejection). No model change, and it matches the owner's rule better than silently changing an edge's meaning — declining an optional feature is conformant under subclause 24.2, but silently reinterpreting one is a defect regardless. Consistent with the existing ErrUndirectedEdge treatment of edgeTypePatternUndirected.

Team-lead's read (2026-07-25): (b) is the likely resolution. Confirm before implementing.

Corpus interaction: the gqlc-h9n.2 corpus **cannot** demand this file, because the UNDIRECTED token is fully discharged by `UNDIRECTED EDGE E (:A)~[:E]~(:B)`, which is a different (already-rejected) construct. So the corpus carries it as a hand-maintained `semanticCases` entry, classified `resolves` today with a reason line saying the corpus cannot detect the defect. **This bead's red is reclassifying that entry to `unsupported`** — do not expect an existing failing test to go green.

title: schema/gql: audit the accepted GQL subset against ISO 39075 — record or remove every deviation
description:
Owner principle (2026-07-24): *"we should be able to accept any valid ISO GQL. we
should not have our own GQLC flavour of ISO GQL."*

Taken at face value, that principle reaches further than the phrase-form bug
(gqlc-uhb). `internal/schema/gql` currently rejects several constructs that **are
valid ISO GQL**:

| Sentinel | Construct | Site |
|---|---|---|
| `ErrLabelImplication` | label implication `=> :Label` | listener.go:132-148 |
| `ErrUndirectedEdge` | undirected edge types | listener.go:150-152 |
| `ErrUnsupportedSource` | graph type `LIKE` source (and `COPY OF`) | listener.go:87-90 |

Each of these is a deliberate, documented-in-code deviation from full ISO GQL.
None is recorded in an ADR. So today the supported GQL subset exists only as
scattered sentinels in one file, which is how the phrase-form gap went unnoticed:
there is no single place that states what gqlc accepts.

## Two deliverables

**1. Decide each deviation.** For every rejection above: either implement it, or
record an ADR justifying the deviation with a concrete reason. Some are likely
legitimate — undirected edges may have no faithful mapping onto the
openCypher/neo4j execution model that the generated code targets, and
`COPY OF`/`LIKE` reference catalog state that a static code generator cannot see.
Those are good reasons to reject. They should be *written down*, not implicit,
so the subset is a decision rather than an accident.

**2. Make unhandled grammar branches impossible to ship.** Enumerate every
alternative of every element-type rule in `GQL.g4` and assert the listener either
handles it or explicitly rejects it. The phrase-form bug existed precisely because
a grammar branch was neither handled nor rejected — it fell through into silence.
A test that fails when a new branch is left unhandled prevents the next one.

Note this is a stronger guarantee than the `ErrEmptyGraphType` guard in
gqlc-uhb. That guard catches the *symptom* (a schema that resolved to nothing);
this catches the *cause* (a branch nobody wired up), including cases where some
declarations resolve and only one form is silently skipped.
acceptance_criteria:
An ADR states the supported graph-type DDL subset in one place, replacing the implicit subset defined by scattered l.fail calls.
Every declined construct is recorded against its Annex D feature ID with the phrasing 'optional feature GGxx not supported because ...', not as a deviation from ISO.
Mandatory features are identified as such and none is declined.
The undirected-edge rejection is grounded in observable nonconformance (IS DIRECTED, IS SOURCE OF) plus GH02 optionality, not in an unrepresentability claim.
The COPY OF rejection is grounded in gqlc's one-graph-type rule and missing catalog namespace, not in offline-ness.
Fabric extensions and GQL-2 prereserved words are recorded as out of scope rather than as gaps.
Every sibling bead's decision is reflected; the ADR lands last in the epic.
notes:
## Evidence gathered 2026-07-25: ErrLabelImplication is a bigger gap than it looks

While researching the endpoint question for gqlc-uhb, two strong independent
sources showed that label implication (`=>`) is not a fringe corner of ISO GQL —
it is the standard's mechanism for **node type hierarchies and property
inheritance**, i.e. a core graph-type modelling feature.

1. Microsoft Fabric's GQL graph types reference (reviewed by Stefan Plantikow, a
   GQL standard editor) uses `=>` throughout, and explains its semantics:
   `(:University => :Organization)` and `(:Company => :Organization)` where
   "`University` and `Company` are the key labels of the two node types defined,
   while `Organization` is a secondary label shared by both". It states that
   "the properties of node types identified by secondary labels are automatically
   inherited when using this syntax", and that one label — the key label — must
   uniquely identify the node type.
   https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/graph/gql-graph-types

2. Alex Miłowski's worked example declares node types the same way:
   `NODE :Person => :Thing { ... } AS Person`.
   https://www.milowski.com/journal/entry/2024-06-26T12:00:00-07:00/

listener.go:132-148 currently rejects every `=>` outright via
`rejectLabelImplication`, so gqlc cannot express any node type hierarchy at all.
Under the no-dialect principle this is the most significant of the three
deviations and probably deserves its own bead once this audit prioritises them.

Also worth noting for the audit's scope: the Fabric page documents `ABSTRACT`
node types and a `+=` inheritance shortcut, and its property types include
`LIST<T>`. Whether those are ISO GQL proper or Fabric extensions needs checking
before treating them as conformance obligations — the page itself cautions that
some syntax it shows "isn't currently supported directly for graph", so it is
documenting the standard's syntax rather than only its own.

title: chore(ci): add live-smoke to master's required status checks
description:
gqlc-rvw (PR #323) landed the CODE half of promoting codegen-live to
PR-blocking — the workflow now runs on every PR. But the CONFIG half is
missing: master's branch-protection required_status_checks.contexts is
still [lint, test, tidy, actionlint, govulncheck]. \`live-smoke\` (the
codegen-live workflow's job name) is NOT in the required list, so it
runs but doesn't block auto-merge.

Proof (PR #323 itself): the live-smoke job was still IN_PROGRESS when
auto-merge fired at 05:37:22Z. Job completed successfully at 05:37:32Z
(10s later) — but had it failed, the merge would have happened anyway.
Wall-time on the runner was 63s (setup-go + setup-just + docker + both
arms in parallel).

Fix (one-line via the GH API):

  gh api -X PATCH \\
    repos/areqag/gqlc/branches/master/protection/required_status_checks \\
    -f 'contexts[]=lint' -f 'contexts[]=test' -f 'contexts[]=tidy' \\
    -f 'contexts[]=actionlint' -f 'contexts[]=govulncheck' \\
    -f 'contexts[]=live-smoke'

Verify: after apply, \`gh api repos/areqag/gqlc/branches/master/protection\`
should include \`live-smoke\` in contexts. Then any PR whose live-smoke
job FAILS will block auto-merge.

Alternative: do this via the GitHub UI at
https://github.com/areqag/gqlc/settings/branches — edit the master rule,
add \`live-smoke\` to required status checks.

This is a shared-infrastructure config change, not a code change — needs
owner action (or explicit owner sign-off before an agent runs the API
call).

Descends from: gqlc-rvw (which shipped the code half in PR #323).
close_reason: Applied via gh api PATCH — master's required_status_checks.contexts now includes live-smoke alongside the existing 5 checks. Verified via GET on branches/master/protection. Any future PR whose live-smoke job fails or is still in-progress will now block auto-merge. The gqlc-rvw promotion is fully complete — both the code half (on.pull_request trigger, PR #323) and the config half (required-checks list).

title: master-guard claude-pre-bash hook false-positives on worktree commits
description: The PreToolUse master-guard hook (.githooks/claude-pre-bash:31) resolves the branch via 'git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD' in the hook's own pwd (the Bash tool's persistent cwd), not the git command's actual target. A 'git -C <worktree> commit' (or a command that cd's inside the worktree within the same call) targeting a feature branch is denied when the session cwd sits on master. Observed 2026-07-14 during gqlc-ls8.2 (commit-5 halt in .claude/worktrees/ls8-2-cypher). Workaround: persistently cd the Bash tool into the worktree so the hook resolves the right branch. Fix direction: make the hook resolve the branch at the command's effective target — parse 'git -C <path>' and leading 'cd <path> &&' from tool_input.command before rev-parse. Needs its own PR + review; do NOT patch mid-loop.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #310 (squash 6a83f0e). PreToolUse master-guard rewritten as a python3 analyzer: effective-target resolution (cd/pushd chains, -C joins), quote-aware heredoc stripping, substitution-body recursion, shlex tokenization kills prose false positives; symbolic-ref fallback covers unborn HEADs. 29-case harness wired into just test (CI parity). Adversarial Linus review: PASS after 2 SHOULD-FIXes applied.

comments.author: antranig-yeretzian
comments.text: Second finding (2026-07-14, same ls8.2 halt): the hook also has a FALSE NEGATIVE. Regex at line 25 requires the word git immediately followed by the word commit, so the form [git -C <path> commit ...] does not match at all and is never branch-checked — this is how the ls8-2 worktree commits (c4deb99..6f2b2c1) landed before the halt. Empirically verified: the bare form and the cd-compound form MATCH (then branch-check the hook pwd -> false positive for worktree work); the -C form passes unchecked. Also noted: the hook matches the raw command string including quoted literals and prose (a for-loop echoing the bare form as a string was denied; so was a bd-comment command whose prose contained it). Fix should: (1) parse -C / leading-cd to resolve the command's effective target dir, (2) branch-check THAT dir, (3) ideally ignore quoted literals. Interim team ruling for ls8.2: worktree commits proceed via the -C form — target branch is cypher-collection-sink, the hook's stated intent (block commits on master/main) is preserved, and repo git hooks (core.hooksPath pre-commit gates) still fire normally. This interim allowance dies when this bead's fix lands.

title: cypher parser: one collection sink replaces 14 per-handler subqueryDepth guards

title: CLI-2: gqlc init — interactive huh wizard for gqlc.yaml

Old-version files migrate naturally (Load normalises, Save writes latest).
